feedback: Formal and informal sport are distinguished mainly by the level of organisation, structure and rules.

q: A student runs from school to the train station because they need to catch a train. Why is this transportation rather than exercise?
options: Running cannot be classified as exercise for school-aged people.
The primary purpose is travelling from one location to another.
The activity is too short to produce any health or fitness benefit.
Transportation must always occur as part of a daily routine.
feedback: Running can fit different categories. Here, its main purpose is travel between destinations, making it transportation.

q: Students play four-square at recess using agreed rules, boundaries and a goal of eliminating opponents. Why is 'game' the most appropriate classification?
options: It occurs during leisure time and therefore must be recreation.
It uses a ball, which means it should be classified as sport.
It is organised around rules and a goal without needing formal sporting structures.
It is spontaneous movement without agreed rules or an objective.
feedback: Games have rules and a goal or objective, but they do not require the formal organisation associated with formal sport.

q: A person dances socially at a community festival during their free time for enjoyment. There is no training goal or competition. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Game
Exercise
Formal sport
Recreational activity
feedback: In this context, dancing is a voluntary leisure activity undertaken for enjoyment, so it is recreational.

q: Activity log: 7:45 am walk to school; 4:00 pm clean the garage; 5:30 pm planned resistance workout; 7:00 pm casual fishing. Which entry is transportation?
options: 7:45 am walk to school
4:00 pm clean the garage
5:30 pm planned resistance workout
7:00 pm casual fishing
feedback: Walking to school is transportation because the movement is used to travel from one destination to another.

q: Activity log: 8:00 am garden maintenance; 10:00 am planned 30-minute run to improve fitness; 1:00 pm beach cricket with flexible rules; 4:00 pm walk to the shops. Which entry is exercise?
options: 8:00 am garden maintenance
10:00 am planned run
1:00 pm beach cricket
4:00 pm walk to the shops
feedback: The planned run is structured and completed specifically to improve fitness, so it is exercise.

q: At a community event, participants can choose from a registered tennis tournament, a guided walk to a museum, casual three-on-three basketball with adjustable rules, or a structured fitness circuit. Which activity is informal sport?
options: Registered tennis tournament
Guided walk to a museum
Casual three-on-three basketball
Structured fitness circuit
feedback: Casual three-on-three basketball with adjustable rules is self-organised and flexible, making it informal sport.

Policy
feedback: A formal workplace rule is a policy-level strategy.

q: Which strategy most directly addresses low confidence as a barrier to physical activity?
options: Provide skill-building sessions that create achievable early success
Ask family members and close friends to provide regular encouragement before and during each planned activity session
Build a new recreation centre
Change local planning regulations
feedback: Skill development and achievable success can improve confidence and self-efficacy, targeting the individual component.

q: Which strategy most directly addresses a lack of social support?
options: Provide information about health benefits
Create peer-supported activity groups
Install more bike racks
Change a school attendance rule
feedback: Peer-supported groups target encouragement, companionship and social support.

q: Which strategy most directly addresses poor access to safe places for physical activity?
options: Teach goal-setting skills
Ask participants to invite friends, relatives and neighbours to join them during regular activity sessions
Improve lighting, paths and access to local facilities
Introduce a recommendation about daily activity
feedback: Improving paths, lighting and facilities directly changes the physical environment.

q: Which strategy most directly targets a policy barrier in a school?
options: Improve students' knowledge of exercise benefits
Encourage students to motivate one another
Install new outdoor fitness equipment
Change school procedures so activity spaces can be used during breaks
feedback: Changing school procedures targets the policy component.

q: A school gives students activity-planning lessons, forms peer walking groups, improves bike storage and permits active travel incentives. Why is this likely stronger than a single strategy?
options: It targets multiple interacting components that influence behaviour.
It removes the need to consider student needs.
It guarantees every student will become active.
It focuses only on the individual component.
feedback: A multicomponent approach can address several interacting influences rather than relying on one factor alone.

q: Which pair of strategies targets the social and physical environment respectively?
options: Goal setting and self-monitoring
Walking buddies and improved park lighting
Education sessions and a school rule
Bike lanes and a workplace procedure
feedback: Walking buddies target the social environment, while improved lighting targets the physical environment.

q: A program provides information about physical activity but participants still report unsafe local streets and no nearby facilities. What is the main weakness?
options: It targets too many components at once and therefore makes the initiative unnecessarily complicated for participants to follow
It focuses too much on policy.
It addresses individual knowledge but not important physical-environment barriers.
It removes social support from the program.
feedback: Information targets the individual component, but unsafe streets and poor facility access are physical-environment barriers that remain unaddressed.

q: A council builds a new path but does not promote it, connect it to destinations or address community safety concerns. Which critique is strongest?
options: The initiative is automatically effective because building new infrastructure always changes community behaviour regardless of other barriers
The initiative targets the individual component only.
The initiative should ignore local barriers once construction is complete.
The physical-environment strategy may be limited because other interacting influences remain unaddressed.
feedback: A physical-environment change may be useful, but its effectiveness can be limited if social, individual or policy barriers remain.

q: Why might the same park encourage physical activity for one person but discourage another?
options: People experience the same environment differently because needs, confidence, safety perceptions and social factors vary.
The Social-Ecological Model assumes environments affect everyone identically.
Physical environments cannot act as barriers.
Only policy determines whether a park is used.
feedback: The same environment can influence people differently because individual and social circumstances vary.

q: Which example best shows interaction across different levels of society?
options: One person privately decides to exercise.
A local school, families and council coordinate an active-travel program.
A person reads an article about fitness and then privately records their thoughts about becoming more physically active
One student buys a new pair of shoes.
feedback: The example involves individuals, social groups and community-level organisations working together.

q: Which scenario best demonstrates reciprocal influence?
options: A person ignores every feature of their environment.
A walking path affects activity, but residents can never influence the path.
Residents use a walking trail more often and then campaign successfully for improved lighting.
Government policy changes behaviour in only one direction.
feedback: The environment influences residents' behaviour, while residents' behaviour and advocacy then help change the environment.

q: A neighbourhood cycling group becomes popular and later persuades the council to add safer bike lanes. What does this illustrate?
options: Only individual factors matter.
Physical activity is unaffected by social groups because social influences cannot change the built or policy environment around them
Policy always changes before behaviour.
People can influence their environment as well as being influenced by it.
feedback: The scenario shows reciprocal influence between people and their surrounding environment.

q: When critiquing a physical activity initiative using the Social-Ecological Model, what should be considered first?
options: Which components are targeted and which relevant barriers or enablers remain unaddressed
Whether the initiative uses the newest technology
Whether the program has the longest duration
Whether all participants receive exactly the same strategy even when they experience different barriers, enablers and environmental conditions
feedback: A strong SEM critique identifies the components targeted and considers whether important barriers and enablers have been addressed.

q: Which design feature is most consistent with the Social-Ecological Model?
options: Use one strategy for every population regardless of context.
Combine strategies across several components and adapt them to the target population.
Focus only on knowledge because behaviour is mainly an individual choice and environmental influences are secondary
Ignore environmental barriers if participants are motivated.
feedback: SEM-informed initiatives usually work across multiple components and should respond to the needs and context of the target population.

q: Why should an initiative consider the needs of its target population?
options: Because all populations experience identical barriers and therefore should receive the same strategy regardless of their context
Because policy strategies are never useful.
Because the same strategy may function as an enabler for some people but not others.
Because only individual factors can be changed.
feedback: Different groups can experience environments and strategies differently, so initiatives should be tailored to relevant needs and barriers.

q: Which feature would most improve the sustainability of a physical activity initiative?
options: Rely entirely on short-term enthusiasm.
Use a strategy that depends on one volunteer only and has no plan for continuation if that person leaves
Ignore cost and access barriers.
Build practical supports across several components that can continue over time.
feedback: Sustainable initiatives use practical, ongoing supports rather than relying on a single short-term influence.

q: Initiative: free beginner sessions, trained peer leaders, improved lighting at the venue, and a council permit allowing evening access. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The initiative addresses all four Social-Ecological Model components.
The initiative addresses only individual and social factors.
The initiative addresses physical environment only.
The initiative does not include a policy strategy.
feedback: Beginner sessions can target individual factors, peer leaders target social environment, lighting targets physical environment, and the council permit targets policy.

q: Initiative: an app provides goal setting and reminders, but users report no safe places nearby to exercise. What is the clearest limitation?
options: The initiative targets too many physical-environment factors.
It targets individual factors but leaves a physical-environment barrier unresolved.
The app is a policy strategy and therefore cannot affect behaviour.
Goal setting belongs to the social environment.
feedback: Goal setting and reminders target the individual component, while lack of safe spaces is a physical-environment barrier.

q: Initiative: students receive encouragement from teachers and friends, but school rules prohibit access to the gym at lunchtime. Which components are most clearly involved?
options: Individual and physical environment
Physical environment and individual
Social environment and policy
Policy and individual
feedback: Encouragement comes from the social environment, while rules about gym access are policy.

q: Initiative: a town builds a walking track. Usage remains low because residents feel unsafe walking alone and do not know where the track connects. Which response best applies the model?
options: Remove the track because physical-environment strategies never work.
Provide only more information about health benefits.
Keep the initiative unchanged because one physical-environment component is enough to address all remaining social and individual barriers
Add social support and clearer environmental information while retaining the track.
feedback: The track addresses the physical environment, but social support and clearer information may address remaining barriers.

q: Program features: skills workshop, buddy system, free equipment access and a workplace rule protecting activity-break time. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The program uses a multicomponent approach that addresses individual, social, physical-environment and policy influences.
The program focuses only on individual motivation.
The program ignores the workplace environment.
The program contains no policy element.
feedback: The four features respectively address individual, social, physical-environment/resource access and policy influences.

q: A school installs bike racks and promotes cycling, but many students live too far away or cannot afford a bike. What does this demonstrate?
options: Bike racks automatically remove every barrier to active travel, regardless of distance, cost, confidence or family circumstances
A strategy can support some people while remaining unsuitable for others because barriers differ.
Physical-environment changes should never be used.
Distance and affordability are policy factors only.
feedback: A strategy can be an enabler for some people but remain ineffective for others when different barriers are present.

q: A council campaign tells residents to 'be more active' but provides no changes to facilities, social support or local policies. Which critique is strongest?
options: The campaign is comprehensive because information addresses every SEM component.
The campaign mainly changes the physical environment.
The campaign mainly targets individual factors and may be limited because other barriers are not addressed.
The campaign is a policy strategy because the council created it.
feedback: Information campaigns primarily target individual knowledge or motivation. Their impact may be limited if social, environmental or policy barriers remain.

q: A workplace wants to reduce prolonged sitting. Which initiative best reflects the Social-Ecological Model?
options: Send one detailed email explaining that prolonged sitting is harmful and expect employees to independently change their daily behaviour
Ask employees to rely on motivation alone.
Install standing desks but make no other changes.
Combine education, team movement breaks, accessible standing options and a procedure supporting regular breaks.
feedback: The strongest option addresses individual knowledge, social support, physical environment and policy together.

q: Which response best explains why multicomponent initiatives are often preferred within the Social-Ecological Model?
options: Physical activity behaviour is shaped by interacting influences, so addressing several components can reduce multiple barriers and strengthen enablers.
Every component must always contribute equally to every person's behaviour.
Policy strategies are always more powerful than individual strategies.
Once one barrier is removed, all remaining influences become irrelevant.
feedback: Because behaviour is influenced by multiple interacting factors, initiatives that address several relevant components can be more comprehensive.

q: A school wants to increase active transport. Which combination best applies the Social-Ecological Model?
options: Give students a brochure and make no other changes.
Teach route-planning skills, organise walking groups, improve bike storage and adopt supportive active-travel procedures.
Build one bike rack without consulting students or families and assume the new facility will address all barriers to active travel
Ask students to set goals but ignore safety and access.
feedback: The combination targets individual skills, social support, physical environment and policy.

q: An initiative increases activity for some residents but not for others because transport, confidence and family support differ. Which SEM principle is best demonstrated?
options: One strategy affects everyone in exactly the same way, regardless of differences in transport, confidence, family support or local environment
Only the physical environment influences behaviour.
Physical activity is shaped by multiple interacting influences that vary between people and contexts.
Population strategies should avoid adapting to different barriers.
feedback: The scenario shows that multiple factors interact and that the same strategy can have different effects across people and settings.

q: A community walking initiative currently provides only weekly group walks. Which modification would best strengthen it using the Social-Ecological Model?
options: Remove the group walks and provide information only.
Keep the program unchanged because social support is sufficient.
Require every participant to follow the same walking target.
Add individual goal support, improve safe walking routes and work with council on supportive access policies.
feedback: Adding individual, physical-environment and policy strategies broadens the existing social strategy into a stronger multicomponent initiative.

q: What is a key purpose of a population-based physical activity initiative?
options: To increase physical activity and/or reduce sedentary behaviour in a selected population
To measure only the fitness of elite athletes
To replace all individual responsibility for physical activity
To focus only on competitive sport performance
feedback: Population-based initiatives aim to increase physical activity and/or reduce sedentary behaviour within a selected group, community or population.

q: Which group could be an appropriate target population for a physical activity initiative?
options: Only professional athletes in organised high-performance sport
Older adults living in a local community
Only people already meeting activity guidelines
Only students enrolled in physical education
feedback: Population-based initiatives may target many different groups, including age-based, cultural, socioeconomic or other population groups.

q: Why should an initiative identify the barriers experienced by its target population?
options: So every participant receives exactly the same strategy
So the initiative can avoid using multiple SEM components
So strategies can be designed to address the factors limiting participation
So only individual motivation needs to be considered
feedback: Identifying relevant barriers helps an initiative select strategies that directly address the reasons participation is limited.

q: Which statement best describes intersectoral collaboration?
options: One participant completing several activities
One organisation delivering a program without support
A program focusing only on individual motivation and personal knowledge
Different sectors working together towards a shared physical activity goal
feedback: Intersectoral collaboration involves different sectors or organisations combining resources, expertise and support towards a common goal.

q: Which feature is most likely to strengthen a population-based physical activity initiative?
options: Addressing several relevant barriers and enablers across multiple SEM components
Using one strategy regardless of the target population
Assuming awareness automatically leads to participation
Ignoring access and resource limitations
feedback: Initiatives are generally stronger when they respond to relevant barriers and enablers across multiple levels of influence.

q: What is one potential benefit of involving several stakeholders in an initiative?
options: It guarantees the initiative will succeed.
It can increase access to expertise, funding, facilities and community connections.
It removes the need to identify barriers within the target population.
It means the initiative only needs one strategy.
feedback: Different stakeholders can contribute complementary resources, expertise, funding, facilities and access to participants.

q: When critiquing an initiative, which evidence is most useful?
options: The initiative's name alone
The organisation's logo
Information about the strategies used, barriers addressed and likely outcomes
The total number of words used to describe the program in promotional materials
feedback: A meaningful critique uses evidence about what the initiative does, which barriers or enablers it targets, and how likely those strategies are to influence participation.

q: Which statement best reflects effective initiative design?
options: All groups require identical strategies.
One short campaign is always enough for lasting behaviour change.
Only policy strategies can change population behaviour.
Different populations may require different strategies because their barriers and enablers differ.
feedback: Population groups can experience different barriers and enablers, so initiative design should be responsive to the target population.

q: A council finds that older adults in one suburb are inactive because they feel unsafe walking alone. Which initiative feature most directly addresses this barrier?
options: Organised local walking groups led at regular times
Posters describing the health benefits of regular exercise
A competitive online leaderboard
A discount for sports equipment
feedback: Walking groups directly address the social and safety-related barrier by providing companionship and structured opportunities to be active.

q: A school wants to increase activity among students who say they lack confidence and do not know how to use the fitness area. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Extend the school day
Provide beginner instruction and supported practice sessions
Remove organised activities and supervised practice opportunities
Require students to exercise independently
feedback: Beginner instruction and supported practice target knowledge, skills and confidence barriers.

q: A community initiative offers free weekend activity sessions in an area where participation costs are a major barrier. Which barrier is being targeted most directly?
options: Fear of judgement
Limited social support
Financial cost
Poor weather
feedback: Free participation directly reduces the financial cost barrier.

q: A local initiative is jointly delivered by a council, health service, sporting club and secondary school. What is the clearest advantage of this collaboration?
options: Every participant will respond in exactly the same way to every strategy used.
The initiative no longer needs to evaluate outcomes.
Only one SEM component needs to be addressed.
The organisations can combine facilities, expertise, participant access and resources.
feedback: Collaboration can increase reach and effectiveness by combining different forms of expertise, infrastructure, access and resources.

q: Step Up to Breast Cancer asks participants to walk or run a set distance during August, allows the distance to be completed across multiple sessions, and lets participants track progress online. Which feature most directly supports different fitness levels?
options: The distance can be completed across multiple sessions.
The challenge occurs in August.
Progress is recorded online.
The initiative is linked to fundraising.
feedback: Allowing the target distance to be accumulated across multiple sessions provides flexibility for participants with different fitness levels.

q: This Girl Can encourages women to be active without fear of judgement and uses relatable stories that challenge stereotypes about women and exercise. Which barrier is most directly targeted?
options: Limited access to suitable sporting facilities
Fear of judgement and gender stereotypes
Insufficient wearable technology
Limited government regulation
feedback: The initiative directly targets psychosocial barriers such as fear of judgement, low confidence and gender stereotypes.

q: Jump Rope for Heart is a school-based program in which students learn skipping skills, participate with peers and receive teacher support. Which strategy most directly builds an individual enabler?
options: Participating alongside classmates
Receiving encouragement from teachers
Learning and practising skipping skills
Using a school activity space
feedback: Learning and practising a skill can increase competence, confidence and self-efficacy at the individual level.

q: The Get Active Kids Voucher Program provides eligible Victorian children with financial assistance towards organised sport and recreation costs. Which barrier does the voucher most directly reduce?
options: Lack of peer encouragement
Low knowledge of activity benefits
Poor local weather
Participation costs
feedback: The voucher directly targets financial barriers such as registration, participation and equipment costs.

q: The 10,000 Steps program allows participants to track steps, set goals and monitor progress through a website or app. Which enabler is most directly strengthened?
options: Motivation and self-monitoring
Access to organised team sport
Government regulation
Availability of indoor facilities
feedback: Goal setting and progress tracking can strengthen motivation, accountability and self-monitoring.

q: The Indigenous Marathon Project selects Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander adults for marathon training, health and leadership education, and mentoring. Graduates can become role models in their communities. Which feature most directly strengthens the social environment?
options: Completing a challenging long-distance marathon training program
Developing supportive networks and community role models
Using training equipment
Receiving program funding
feedback: Support networks, mentoring and role models are social-environment influences.

q: An initiative successfully raises awareness about physical activity but participation does not increase because transport and cost barriers remain. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: Awareness is always sufficient to change behaviour even when major practical barriers to participation remain.
The initiative should stop collecting data.
The initiative addresses knowledge but does not adequately address important access barriers.
The target population should simply become more motivated.
feedback: Increasing awareness may help, but participation can remain limited when practical barriers such as transport and cost are not addressed.

q: A free community exercise program attracts many participants for four weeks, but attendance falls sharply after the program ends. Which limitation is most evident?
options: The initiative targeted too many people.
The sessions were free.
The program should have avoided all social support and relied only on participants' own motivation.
The short-term program may not have supported lasting behaviour change.
feedback: A decline after the program ends suggests a limitation in sustainability and long-term behaviour change.

q: Young people in a rural town report limited facilities, transport difficulties and few organised activities. Which response best matches their barriers?
options: Provide local low-cost activities, transport support and access to suitable community spaces.
Run an online awareness campaign only.
Ask participants to set personal goals without changing access.
Introduce a competitive ranking system.
feedback: The most suitable response directly addresses multiple access barriers rather than relying only on individual motivation.

q: A council provides a park, a health organisation trains leaders, and a local community group recruits participants for weekly activity sessions. Why is this an example of intersectoral collaboration?
options: All organisations are performing the same role in delivery.
Different organisations contribute complementary resources towards one shared goal.
The initiative targets only individual motivation.
No target population has been identified.
feedback: Intersectoral collaboration involves different sectors contributing different strengths and resources towards a common objective.

q: A program for parents of young children identifies childcare and time as major barriers to physical activity. Which strategy best responds to these barriers?
options: Provide information about exercise guidelines only.
Create a national advertising slogan.
Offer short activity sessions with on-site childcare at convenient times.
Use a step-count competition with no childcare, schedule changes or other practical support.
feedback: Convenient session times and childcare directly address the identified time and caregiving barriers.

q: An initiative provides a mobile app for activity tracking to a low-income population, but many intended participants do not have reliable smartphone or data access. What is the most important limitation?
options: The initiative uses a mobile app rather than printed promotional posters and leaflets.
The program collects activity information.
Participants can set goals.
Digital access may exclude part of the target population.
feedback: A strategy is less accessible when members of the target population cannot reliably use the technology required.

q: One initiative provides financial assistance for sport fees, while another provides peer-led walking groups. What best explains the difference in approach?
options: They target different barriers to participation.
Only one can be a population-based initiative.
Financial strategies never affect participation.
Social support is always more effective than cost reduction.
feedback: Different initiatives may use different strategies because their target populations experience different barriers and enablers.

q: Which evidence would best help determine whether an initiative has increased physical activity in its target population?
options: The program's promotional slogan
Participation or activity data collected before and after the initiative
The colour of the program logo
The number of organisations listed on the website and the length of each organisation's description
feedback: Pre- and post-initiative participation or activity data provide direct evidence of whether physical activity changed.

q: A program is popular with participants but only reaches a very small proportion of the intended population. Which aspect of effectiveness is most limited?
options: Enjoyment among participants who already chose to attend the program sessions
Individual goal setting
Reach across the target population
Use of social support
feedback: If only a small proportion of the target population participates, the initiative has limited reach.

q: Which initiative is most likely to be sustainable?
options: A one-off event with no follow-up, no local partnerships and no plan for maintaining participation after the event ends
A program that relies on one short-term volunteer
A campaign that ignores funding and staffing requirements
An initiative with ongoing resources, local partnerships and practical strategies that can continue over time
feedback: Sustainability is strengthened by ongoing resources, partnerships and practical strategies that can continue beyond a short campaign.

q: Initiative: a local program for women provides beginner activity sessions, female peer leaders, free venue access and childcare during sessions. Which statement best explains why the initiative may be effective?
options: It addresses several barriers and enablers rather than relying on one strategy.
It assumes every participant experiences the same barrier.
It focuses only on policy.
It removes the need to evaluate participation.
feedback: The initiative addresses confidence, social support, access and childcare barriers through multiple strategies.

q: Initiative: a council promotes a new walking trail through social media, but residents report the trail has poor lighting and feels unsafe after work. What is the clearest weakness?
options: The initiative provides too much physical-environment support.
It promotes awareness without adequately addressing the safety barrier.
The target population has no relevant barriers.
Social media automatically guarantees participation even when environmental barriers remain unresolved.
feedback: Promotion may increase awareness, but the unresolved safety issue remains a significant physical-environment barrier.

q: Initiative: a school offers free lunchtime dance sessions after students report cost and lack of enjoyable options as barriers. Attendance increases substantially. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Cost was the only possible barrier and no other factor could have contributed to the increase in attendance.
The initiative proves all schools should use dance.
The strategies appear to address identified barriers and are associated with increased participation.
The increase must have resulted from policy change.
feedback: The initiative directly addresses cost and activity-choice barriers, and the rise in attendance supports a positive effect on participation.

q: Initiative: eligible children receive a voucher for sport fees, but families still report difficulty reaching training venues. Which improvement is most appropriate?
options: Increase advertising about the health benefits of sport without addressing the transport problem described.
Remove the financial assistance.
Require children to participate more often.
Add transport support or more locally accessible activity options.
feedback: The voucher addresses financial cost, but transport remains an access barrier requiring an additional strategy.

q: Initiative: adults use a free step-tracking app, can join team challenges and receive suggestions for local walking routes. Which feature targets the social environment?
options: Team challenges that encourage participants to support one another
Step tracking within the app to monitor daily movement and progress towards personal goals
Suggestions for nearby walking routes
Free access to the digital tool
feedback: Team challenges create social support, encouragement and interaction between participants.

q: Initiative: a culturally specific running program provides coaching, mentoring, travel support and leadership education to a small selected group. Which limitation is most directly indicated by the description?
options: The program provides no support.
The initiative has limited reach because participation is restricted to a small selected group.
The program cannot influence confidence.
The initiative has no target population because culturally specific programs are intended to include every member of the community.
feedback: A small selected cohort can receive intensive support, but the program's direct reach across the broader population is limited.

q: A program for secondary students provides activity information and goal-setting tools, but students identify cost, transport and lack of peer support as their main barriers. Which critique is strongest?
options: The program is effective because individual strategies always overcome financial, transport and social barriers when participants are sufficiently motivated.
The initiative should remove goal setting because it is never useful.
The program targets individual factors but leaves several important participation barriers unaddressed.
The target population should be changed instead of the strategies.
feedback: Information and goal setting target individual factors, but the stated financial, transport and social barriers remain.

q: A community wants to increase physical activity among older adults who report low confidence, social isolation and poor access to safe walking spaces. Which initiative best addresses these barriers?
options: Send a detailed brochure explaining the benefits of exercise and expect older adults to overcome confidence, isolation and access barriers independently.
Run a one-day fitness competition.
Ask participants to independently track steps at home.
Provide beginner walking sessions, trained group leaders and safe accessible routes in partnership with council.
feedback: The strongest initiative directly addresses confidence, social isolation and environmental access using coordinated strategies.

q: A statewide campaign encourages women to be active and provides stories from diverse participants, flexible activity ideas and links to welcoming local providers. Why may this be more effective than awareness messaging alone?
options: It combines confidence-building messages with practical and socially supportive opportunities to participate.
It guarantees that cost and childcare barriers are removed for every woman.
It targets only the policy component of the SEM.
It avoids the need to consider barriers within different communities.
feedback: The campaign goes beyond awareness by also supporting confidence, practical access and connection with welcoming participation opportunities.

q: A youth activity initiative is developed by a school, local council and community sporting organisation. The school recruits students, the council provides facilities and the organisation supplies coaches. What is the best explanation of this approach?
options: Each stakeholder duplicates the same role.
Intersectoral collaboration allows different organisations to contribute complementary resources and expertise.
The program is effective only because a school is involved.
Collaboration removes the need to identify barriers because partner organisations can assume the program will suit every student.
feedback: The organisations contribute different resources and capabilities, which is the central benefit of intersectoral collaboration.

q: A four-week walking challenge records high participation during the program, but follow-up data show activity levels return to baseline two months later. Which evaluation is best supported?
options: The initiative was ineffective during the four weeks because activity returned to baseline after the program ended.
The initiative had no reach.
The initiative achieved short-term participation but showed limited evidence of sustained behaviour change.
The initiative should be judged only by its advertising reach.
feedback: High participation during the program indicates short-term impact, while the return to baseline suggests limited sustainability.

q: A council plans an initiative for teenagers who report low confidence, lack of transport and few affordable activities. Which proposal best reflects effective population-based initiative design?
options: Provide motivational posters only.
Build one facility without consulting young people.
Ask teenagers to take responsibility for overcoming all barriers themselves.
Co-design low-cost local activities, provide beginner support and improve transport or local access with community partners.
feedback: The proposal responds directly to the identified confidence, cost and access barriers and uses multiple coordinated strategies.

q: Which health-related fitness component is defined as the maximum rate of energy production from the aerobic energy system?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength produced during a single maximal effort
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Aerobic power is the maximum rate of energy production from the aerobic energy system.

q: Which health-related fitness component is the peak force that a muscle can develop?
options: Aerobic power used during prolonged continuous physical activity
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Muscular strength is the peak force that a muscle can develop.

q: Which component is the ability of a muscle or muscle group to sustain repeated or sustained contractions against resistance for an extended period?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Muscular endurance involves sustaining repeated or sustained contractions against resistance over an extended period.

q: Which health-related fitness component is the range of movement around a joint?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Flexibility is the range of movement around a joint.

q: Which factor is most likely to increase aerobic power?
options: A greater proportion of slow-twitch muscle fibres
A greater proportion of fast-twitch muscle fibres
A reduction in haemoglobin levels
A reduction in lung elasticity
feedback: Slow-twitch fibres work aerobically, so a greater proportion can increase the ability to produce energy aerobically.

q: Which factor is most likely to increase a person's potential muscular strength?
options: A smaller muscle cross-sectional area
A larger muscle cross-sectional area
A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres
A faster muscle contraction in every situation
feedback: A larger muscle cross-sectional area provides greater potential to produce force.

q: Which factor is most likely to increase muscular endurance?
options: A greater proportion of fast-twitch fibres
A lower tolerance to metabolic by-products
A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres
A reduction in aerobic capacity
feedback: Slow-twitch fibres are fatigue resistant and support repeated contractions over longer periods.

q: Which factor is most likely to increase flexibility immediately before activity?
options: Increasing age
Shortened muscles at rest
A joint designed mainly for stability
An effective warm-up
feedback: A warm-up increases the temperature of muscles and structures around joints, which can increase flexibility.

q: A student wants to cycle to school without tiring as quickly. Which fitness component is most directly involved?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Cycling for a continuous period relies heavily on aerobic energy production, so aerobic power is particularly important.

q: A person needs to lift a heavy box from the floor once. Which fitness component is most important for producing the required force?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: A single heavy lift requires high force production, so muscular strength is the most relevant component.

q: A student completes repeated push-ups for several minutes. Which fitness component is being used most directly?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Repeated push-ups require the muscles to continue contracting against resistance, which relies on muscular endurance.

q: A gardener needs to bend safely through a large range of movement at the hip. Which fitness component is most relevant?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: Flexibility allows a joint to move through an appropriate range of motion.

q: Two people complete the same long-distance run. One has a greater proportion of slow-twitch muscle fibres. What effect is this most likely to have?
options: Greater aerobic power and improved ability to sustain aerobic work
Lower aerobic power because slow-twitch fibres fatigue quickly during continuous activity and cannot sustain repeated contractions
Greater peak force during a single maximal contraction
Reduced oxygen use by the working muscles
feedback: Slow-twitch fibres have strong aerobic characteristics and resist fatigue, supporting sustained aerobic activity.

q: Why does aerobic power generally decrease with increasing age after early adulthood?
options: Muscles always become larger with age.
Changes such as reduced lung elasticity, haemoglobin and muscle mass can reduce oxygen uptake, transport and use.
Older adults automatically stop using aerobic energy.
Flexibility becomes the only limiting fitness component.
feedback: Age-related reductions in lung elasticity, haemoglobin and muscle mass can reduce the body's capacity to take in, transport and use oxygen.

q: A student improves leg muscle size after resistance training. Which change is most likely to increase their potential muscular strength?
options: A lower muscle temperature
A smaller joint range of motion
A larger muscle cross-sectional area
A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres
feedback: A larger muscle cross-sectional area increases the potential for greater force production.

q: Which statement best explains how muscle contraction speed affects muscular strength?
options: Faster contractions always produce greater force because increased movement speed automatically increases the force produced by a muscle
Contraction speed has no effect on force.
Only isometric contractions can produce force.
Slower contractions can generally produce greater force than faster contractions.
feedback: The force-velocity relationship means muscles generally produce greater force at slower contraction speeds.

q: Why can a warm-up improve muscular strength performance?
options: Warmer muscles are better prepared to produce force.
Warm-ups permanently increase muscle cross-sectional area and therefore create a lasting increase in maximum force production
Warm-ups convert slow-twitch fibres into fast-twitch fibres.
Warm-ups remove the effect of joint angle.
feedback: Warming the muscles can improve their capacity to contract and produce force during activity.

q: Which person is most likely to have greater potential for absolute muscular strength, assuming other factors are similar?
options: A person with less muscle mass
A person with greater muscle mass
A person with more adipose tissue but the same muscle mass
A person with a smaller muscle cross-sectional area
feedback: Greater muscle mass and cross-sectional area generally provide greater potential for absolute muscular strength.

q: A person can tolerate a greater accumulation of metabolic by-products during repeated high-intensity efforts. What is the likely effect?
options: Reduced flexibility because greater tolerance to metabolic by-products decreases the range of movement available around the working joints
Reduced aerobic power
Improved muscular endurance during repeated high-intensity work
Lower muscular strength in every contraction
feedback: Greater tolerance to metabolic by-products can allow high-intensity muscular work to continue for longer.

q: Why does a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres support muscular endurance?
options: They produce the highest peak force.
They fatigue more quickly during repeated work.
They prevent any metabolic by-products from forming.
They are relatively fatigue resistant and can sustain aerobic contractions for longer.
feedback: Slow-twitch fibres resist fatigue and are well suited to repeated or sustained contractions.

q: A person spends long periods sitting and develops chronically shortened hamstrings. What is the most likely effect?
options: Reduced flexibility at joints influenced by the shortened muscles
Increased aerobic power because sitting for long periods improves the body's ability to take in, transport and use oxygen
Increased peak muscular force
Greater muscular endurance
feedback: Shortened muscles can restrict range of movement and therefore reduce flexibility.

q: Why does joint type affect flexibility?
options: All joints have the same structure but different temperatures, so mobility depends mainly on how warm the surrounding tissues become
Different joints are designed with different balances of mobility and stability.
Joint type affects only muscular strength.
Joint type changes the proportion of muscle fibre types.
feedback: Joint structure influences how much movement is possible; some joints prioritise mobility while others prioritise stability.

q: Which change is most likely to reduce flexibility over time?
options: Regular movement through a full range
An effective warm-up
Increasing age
Appropriate stretching
feedback: Flexibility generally decreases with increasing age.

q: A person begins a stretching program that gradually lengthens muscles and surrounding connective tissues. What is the most likely effect?
options: Lower aerobic power
Lower muscular endurance because stretching the surrounding tissues prevents the muscles from sustaining repeated contractions against resistance
Smaller muscle cross-sectional area
Increased range of movement around the relevant joint
feedback: Increasing the resting length of muscles and surrounding structures can increase joint range of movement.

q: A tennis player needs to continue moving throughout a long match and repeatedly sustain rallies. Which combination is especially important?
options: Aerobic power and muscular endurance
Muscular strength and flexibility only
Flexibility and peak force only
Muscular strength and reaction time
feedback: Long-duration movement relies on aerobic power, while repeated sustained muscular work relies on muscular endurance.

q: Which example best distinguishes muscular strength from muscular endurance?
options: Both involve only joint range of motion and therefore depend mainly on the flexibility available around the working joints
Strength focuses on peak force, whereas endurance focuses on sustaining repeated or prolonged muscular work.
Strength uses oxygen while endurance never does.
Endurance is required only in cardiovascular exercise.
feedback: Muscular strength concerns maximum force production, while muscular endurance concerns sustaining muscular work over time.

q: Why should a balanced physical activity plan include activities that develop several health-related fitness components?
options: Because every activity develops all four components equally, so selecting a range of activities simply repeats the same fitness effect
Because only sporting performance matters
Because general health and fitness depend on more than one component
Because flexibility is the only component linked to injury risk
feedback: A balanced physical activity plan supports general health and fitness by addressing multiple fitness components.

q: Which statement best distinguishes a physical activity plan from a training program?
options: A physical activity plan is always more intense.
A training program never develops fitness.
Both have exactly the same purpose.
A physical activity plan generally promotes broad health and fitness, while a training program more narrowly targets performance.
feedback: Physical activity plans usually focus on broad health and guideline adherence, while training programs are more performance-specific.

q: A student can jog continuously for longer than before and reports less fatigue during a 20-minute run. Which fitness component has most likely improved?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Flexibility
Peak force
feedback: Being able to sustain continuous aerobic activity with less fatigue is consistent with improved aerobic power.

q: A student increases their one-repetition maximum squat after several weeks of resistance training. Which fitness component has most directly improved?
options: Flexibility
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Aerobic power
feedback: A one-repetition maximum reflects the ability to produce high force, so it is a measure of muscular strength.

q: A student increases from 18 to 30 continuous push-ups without changing technique. Which fitness component has most directly improved?
options: Flexibility
Aerobic power
Muscular endurance
Muscular strength
feedback: Completing more repeated contractions before fatigue indicates improved muscular endurance.

q: A student can now move their shoulder through a greater pain-free range after a stretching program. Which fitness component has most directly improved?
options: Aerobic power
Muscular strength
Muscular endurance
Flexibility
feedback: A greater range of movement around a joint indicates improved flexibility.

q: Two participants have similar training histories. Participant A has a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres and performs better in a prolonged cycling task. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Slow-twitch fibres support aerobic energy production and resist fatigue, benefiting prolonged activity.
Slow-twitch fibres create the greatest peak force during maximal lifting.
Slow-twitch fibres reduce the need for oxygen.
Slow-twitch fibres prevent all muscular fatigue.
feedback: Slow-twitch fibres are well suited to aerobic work and have high fatigue resistance, supporting prolonged activity.

q: A participant performs a flexibility test before and after an effective warm-up and records a greater range of motion afterwards. What best explains the change?
options: The warm-up permanently changed bone structure and therefore created a lasting increase in the amount of movement available at the joint
Increased temperature in muscles and joint structures temporarily improved flexibility.
The warm-up increased muscle cross-sectional area.
The warm-up converted fast-twitch fibres to slow-twitch fibres.
feedback: An effective warm-up raises tissue temperature and can temporarily improve range of movement.

q: A 22-year-old runner has a high proportion of slow-twitch fibres and regularly completes endurance training. Which factor most directly supports their aerobic power according to the fitness-component factors studied?
options: High joint stability because a more stable joint always increases oxygen delivery and therefore directly raises aerobic energy production
Large adipose stores
A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres
A faster muscle contraction speed
feedback: A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres supports aerobic metabolism and is a factor associated with higher aerobic power.

q: A student wants to improve the maximum force produced in a single lift. Which characteristic would most strongly support this goal?
options: A greater proportion of slow-twitch fibres
A shorter resting muscle length in every muscle
Lower muscle temperature
A larger muscle cross-sectional area
feedback: A larger muscle cross-sectional area increases the potential for force production and therefore muscular strength.

q: A participant holds a plank for 45 seconds, rests, and repeats this several times. Which explanation best links the activity to muscular endurance?
options: The abdominal muscles must sustain contraction against resistance over time and resist fatigue.
The abdominal muscles produce one maximal contraction only.
The activity mainly tests range of movement around the spine.
The activity depends only on aerobic power.
feedback: Holding and repeating a plank requires sustained muscular contractions and resistance to fatigue, which are features of muscular endurance.

q: A person has limited shoulder movement because the joint structure prioritises stability and the surrounding tissues are tight. Which statement best explains their flexibility?
options: Flexibility is unaffected by joint structure.
Both joint structure and the resting length of surrounding tissues can limit range of movement.
Only aerobic power determines joint range.
Muscular strength always increases flexibility.
feedback: Flexibility is influenced by joint structure and by the length and elasticity of muscles, ligaments and surrounding tissues.

q: A student is choosing activities for a balanced physical activity plan. Which option best develops all four health-related fitness components across the week?
options: Only short maximal lifts
Only static stretching
Continuous cycling, resistance exercise, repeated body-weight work and flexibility activities
Only low-intensity walking
feedback: The combination develops aerobic power, muscular strength, muscular endurance and flexibility.

q: A person improves their ability to carry heavy objects once, complete repeated push-ups and reach further during a flexibility test. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Only aerobic power has improved.
Only muscular strength has improved.
All improvements reflect the same fitness component.
The results indicate changes in muscular strength, muscular endurance and flexibility respectively.
feedback: A heavy one-off effort reflects muscular strength, repeated push-ups reflect muscular endurance, and increased range of movement reflects flexibility.

q: What is the main purpose of a Functional Movement Assessment (FMA)?
options: To observe movement quality and help inform a safe, suitable physical activity plan
To diagnose musculoskeletal injuries and prescribe appropriate medical treatment for each individual participant
To measure only aerobic fitness
To rank participants by sporting ability
feedback: An FMA observes how a participant performs movements so the results can help inform safe and appropriate physical activity planning.

q: Which factor is primarily a physiological consideration when selecting an FMA?
options: Peer encouragement
Current injury status
Cultural expectations
Confidence during observation
feedback: Physiological considerations include factors such as current fitness, injuries and health conditions.

q: Which factor is primarily a psychological consideration before conducting an FMA?
options: Access to reliable transport and suitable facilities for attending the assessment at the scheduled time
Previous knee surgery
Confidence about completing the assessment
Family expectations
feedback: Psychological considerations include mental and emotional factors such as confidence, motivation and self-efficacy.

q: Which factor is primarily a sociocultural consideration when planning an FMA?
options: Resting heart rate and current cardiovascular responses measured before the participant begins any assessment movement
Joint pain
Movement efficiency
Family or cultural expectations about participation
feedback: Sociocultural considerations include family, peers, community, gender, socioeconomic circumstances, cultural beliefs and traditions.

q: What is the main purpose of pre-participation health screening before an FMA?
options: To identify health or injury information that may affect whether movements are safe and appropriate
To diagnose every medical condition
To guarantee the participant will avoid injury
To replace informed consent
feedback: Pre-participation screening helps identify relevant health conditions, injuries or risks that may require movement modification, referral or additional caution.

q: Which statement is an essential feature of informed consent?
options: The participant must complete every movement once testing begins.
The participant should understand the assessment, possible risks and their right to withdraw.
Only the final score needs to be explained.
Consent is unnecessary when an assessment seems low risk and the participant has exercised before
feedback: Informed consent requires the participant to understand what will occur, relevant risks and their right to withdraw without penalty.

q: What does validity mean when evaluating an FMA?
options: The assessment produces the same score every time.
The assessor uses expensive equipment.
The assessment measures what it claims to measure.
The results are recorded quickly.
feedback: Validity refers to whether an assessment actually measures the movement characteristic it is intended to measure.

q: What does reliability mean when evaluating an FMA?
options: The assessment uses several different movements selected to represent all major areas of the body
The participant receives immediate feedback.
The assessor explains the purpose of the FMA.
The assessment can be repeated under similar conditions with consistent results.
feedback: Reliability is the ability of an assessment to produce consistent results when repeated under similar conditions.

q: Which description best matches accuracy in an FMA?
options: How close the recorded result is to the participant's actual movement ability
How many different movements, body regions and movement patterns are included across the complete assessment
How often the assessment is repeated
How confident the participant feels
feedback: Accuracy concerns how close the recorded result is to the actual ability or characteristic being assessed.

q: A participant reports ongoing knee pain from a previous injury. What is the most appropriate response when selecting FMA movements?
options: Ignore the pain if the participant is motivated.
Select or modify movements to avoid unnecessary knee stress and consider referral if required.
Include deeper knee-flexion movements to test pain tolerance.
Cancel all physical activity indefinitely.
feedback: The FMA should be adapted to the participant's physiological circumstances so testing is safe and appropriate.

q: A participant is anxious about being watched by classmates during an FMA. Which strategy best addresses this psychological consideration?
options: Increase the assessment difficulty.
Ask classmates to give continuous feedback and encouragement throughout every movement in the assessment
Conduct the assessment in a more private setting.
Remove the pre-participation screen.
feedback: Greater privacy can reduce anxiety and support psychological safety during the assessment.

q: A participant says a particular testing arrangement conflicts with an important cultural preference. What should the assessor do?
options: Proceed because all participants should complete exactly the same testing arrangement regardless of individual preferences
Exclude the participant from the entire program.
Ignore the concern unless it changes the final score.
Adapt the assessment where possible while preserving its purpose and safety.
feedback: Sociocultural considerations should inform how an FMA is conducted so the assessment is appropriate, inclusive and respectful.

q: A pre-participation screen identifies unexplained chest pain during exercise. What is the most appropriate next step before conducting a demanding FMA?
options: Seek appropriate medical clearance or advice before proceeding.
Continue because the FMA is not a fitness test.
Ask the participant to sign a stronger consent form.
Use a more difficult movement to confirm the problem.
feedback: Potentially significant health concerns identified during screening should be addressed before demanding physical assessment proceeds.

q: Why is information about previous injuries useful before selecting FMA movements?
options: It guarantees every selected movement will be valid, reliable and accurate for the participant
It helps identify movements that may need to be modified or avoided for safety.
It determines the participant's motivation.
It replaces the need to observe movement technique.
feedback: Previous injuries can affect movement choice and may indicate that particular movements require modification or should be avoided.

q: Which information should be provided before a participant gives informed consent for an FMA?
options: Only the final score they are expected to achieve
Only the name of the assessor
The nature of the assessment, relevant risks, how information will be used and the right to withdraw
A guarantee that no discomfort will occur
feedback: Valid informed consent depends on the participant receiving enough information to make a voluntary, informed decision.

q: A participant decides halfway through an FMA that they no longer want to continue. What should happen?
options: They should finish because consent cannot be withdrawn once testing begins.
They should complete only the remaining low-risk movements.
They should continue if the assessor believes the data are important.
The assessment should stop because consent can be withdrawn.
feedback: A participant has the right to withdraw consent, so the assessment should stop.

q: An FMA claims to assess whole-body functional movement but includes only lower-body movements. What is the main problem?
options: Its validity is limited because the assessment does not adequately represent whole-body movement.
Its reliability is automatically high.
Its accuracy is guaranteed because several different lower-body movements are included and scored using the same system
Its informed-consent process is invalid.
feedback: An assessment should measure what it claims to measure. A whole-body FMA needs movements that adequately represent the whole body.

q: A participant repeats an FMA one week later. Which change would most threaten reliability?
options: Using the same movement sequence, instructions, recovery periods and environmental conditions as the first assessment
Changing the warm-up, movement order and recovery periods
Testing at a similar time of day
Using the same instructions
feedback: Changing testing conditions makes it harder to determine whether score differences reflect real change or inconsistent procedure.

q: Which action is most likely to improve the accuracy of an FMA?
options: Allowing each assessor to invent their own scoring rules
Changing equipment between participants
Using trained assessors, clear protocols and suitable equipment
Removing all rest periods
feedback: Accurate assessment is supported by trained administrators, clear procedures, appropriate equipment and suitable testing conditions.

q: Why should the same movement sequence be used when an FMA is repeated?
options: To make the assessment longer
To increase the participant's motivation
To ensure every movement is harder the second time
To reduce procedural variation and improve consistency between assessments
feedback: Keeping the movement sequence consistent reduces unwanted variation and improves reliability.

q: A participant has low confidence, limited exercise experience and no current injuries. Which FMA approach is most appropriate?
options: Use clear instructions, manageable movements and a supportive setting matched to the participant's ability.
Use advanced movements immediately to reveal weaknesses.
Ignore confidence because it is unrelated to movement assessment.
Use only the participant's age to choose the assessment.
feedback: An appropriate FMA considers physiological and psychological characteristics, including current ability and confidence.

q: A group includes participants with different physical abilities and movement limitations. What is the best justification for modifying parts of the FMA?
options: Modifications make reliability irrelevant.
Adjustments can improve safety and suitability while still assessing relevant movement patterns.
All participants must complete identical movements regardless of injury history, physical ability or potential safety concerns
Modified movements automatically increase every participant's score.
feedback: An FMA should be appropriate for the target individual or group; safe modifications may be justified when they preserve the purpose of the assessment.

q: Which participant factor is most clearly psychological rather than physiological or sociocultural?
options: A previous ankle injury
Family support for physical activity
Self-efficacy about completing unfamiliar movements
Access to transport
feedback: Self-efficacy is a psychological factor describing belief in one's ability to perform successfully.

q: Which participant factor is most clearly sociocultural?
options: Current muscular soreness following recent exercise that may temporarily affect how the participant performs movement tasks
Resting heart rate
Confidence when attempting a squat
Family expectations that influence willingness to participate
feedback: Family expectations are a sociocultural influence because they arise from the participant's social environment.

q: Why should an assessor follow a clear, standardised protocol during an FMA?
options: It supports reliability and accuracy by reducing unnecessary variation in how the assessment is conducted.
It guarantees the FMA is valid for every possible participant, movement characteristic and physical activity planning purpose
It removes the need for informed consent.
It ensures all participants receive the same score.
feedback: Standardised procedures help minimise measurement error and make repeated results more comparable.

q: Two assessors give very different scores for the same movement because they interpret the scoring criteria differently. Which quality is most directly weakened?
options: Validity
Reliability
Participant motivation
Informed consent
feedback: If scoring is inconsistent between assessors, the assessment is less reliable because results cannot be reproduced consistently.

q: An assessor records a movement score incorrectly because the measuring equipment was poorly calibrated. Which quality is most directly affected?
options: Sociocultural suitability
Validity
Accuracy
Psychological safety
feedback: Poorly calibrated or unsuitable equipment can make recorded results less accurate.

q: An FMA is repeated under identical conditions and produces very similar scores, but it does not assess the movement characteristic it claims to measure. Which statement is correct?
options: It is valid but inaccurate.
It is accurate because scores remain similar
It is valid because it is repeatable.
It may be reliable but lacks validity.
feedback: An assessment can be consistent without measuring the intended characteristic. Reliability does not guarantee validity.

q: A 16-year-old participant reports a previous shoulder injury, low confidence when being observed and strong family support for physical activity. Which set of considerations is represented?
options: Physiological, psychological and sociocultural respectively
Psychological, physiological and policy respectively
Sociocultural, psychological and physiological respectively
Physiological, policy and physical-environment respectively
feedback: The injury is physiological, confidence is psychological and family support is sociocultural.

q: Before an FMA, a participant reports knee pain during deep bending. Which response best uses this information?
options: Ignore the pain because the assessor needs standardised data.
Select a safer alternative movement or modify the range while preserving the assessment purpose.
Ask the participant to perform extra repetitions.
Use the pain response as the final FMA score.
feedback: Health-screening information should inform movement selection so the assessment remains safe and appropriate.

q: An assessor repeats an FMA but changes the warm-up, room temperature and recovery time between movements. The participant's scores change substantially. What is the main concern?
options: The FMA is highly valid because environmental conditions were deliberately varied between the two assessment sessions
The participant did not give consent.
Reliability is weakened because testing conditions were not consistent.
The assessment must be diagnostically inaccurate.
feedback: Changes in warm-up, environment and recovery create procedural variation that can reduce reliability.

q: An FMA designed to assess whole-body movement uses squats, lunges, pushing, pulling and overhead movement patterns. Which assessment quality is this broad movement selection most directly supporting?
options: Confidentiality
Reliability
Accuracy of equipment
Validity
feedback: Including movements that represent the claimed construct supports validity.

q: A participant is told what movements will be performed, the possible risks, how results will be used and that they may stop at any time. What process is being demonstrated?
options: Informed consent
Pre-participation screening
Reliability testing
Movement diagnosis
feedback: Explaining the assessment, risks, data use and right to withdraw are core elements of informed consent.

q: A tester follows the correct protocol but uses a damaged measuring device that consistently overstates the result. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The FMA must be valid because the same device is used.
The damaged device threatens accuracy even if the procedure is consistent.
The FMA becomes more reliable because every score is higher.
The participant's motivation is the main problem.
feedback: A consistently faulty device can still produce repeatable results, but the results may not be close to the true value, reducing accuracy.

q: A student with a recent ankle injury, moderate confidence and strong peer support is completing an FMA. Which justification best demonstrates appropriate assessment planning?
options: Use the same advanced movements as everyone else because standardisation is more important than safety.
Focus only on peer support because sociocultural considerations override physiological factors.
Modify movements that load the injured ankle while using supportive instructions and an appropriate testing environment.
Remove all lower-body movements even if some could be completed safely.
feedback: Appropriate planning considers the injury, psychological state and supportive context while preserving safe and relevant assessment.

q: A school repeats an FMA after six weeks. The same assessor uses the same instructions, movement order, recovery periods and testing area. What is the main reason for doing this?
options: To increase validity by adding more movements
To make the participant more confident
To remove the need for accurate equipment
To improve reliability so changes are more likely to reflect the participant rather than testing variation
feedback: Keeping procedures consistent improves reliability and makes pre- and post-assessment comparisons more meaningful.

q: An assessor wants to evaluate whole-body functional movement. Which option provides the strongest evidence of validity?
options: The assessment samples several relevant movement patterns across different parts of the body.
The same stopwatch is used for every participant.
Participants are tested at the same time of day using the same instructions and recovery periods
The assessor records results immediately.
feedback: Validity depends on whether the assessment adequately measures the intended construct; a whole-body FMA should represent whole-body movement.

q: A participant completes an FMA in a crowded public space and appears embarrassed, rushed and unwilling to attempt unfamiliar movements. Which change is most appropriate?
options: Increase the number of observers to improve scoring accuracy.
Use a more private and supportive setting to reduce psychological discomfort and improve engagement.
Ignore the response because psychological factors do not affect how confidently or willingly a participant completes unfamiliar movements
Replace the FMA with a medical diagnosis.
feedback: The participant's psychological state should inform how the FMA is conducted; privacy and support may improve comfort and willingness to participate.

q: A participant signs a form but was not told about possible risks or their right to withdraw. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: The consent is fully informed because obtaining a participant's signature is sufficient even when risks and withdrawal rights were not explained
The assessment is reliable because documentation exists.
The consent process is inadequate because important information was not provided before agreement.
The FMA is invalid because the participant signed the form.
feedback: A signature alone is insufficient; informed consent requires relevant information to be provided before a voluntary decision is made.

q: An FMA produces consistent scores across repeated trials, uses a suitable range of movements, but the assessor frequently records measurements incorrectly. Which conclusion is best?
options: The assessment is accurate because it is repeatable.
The assessment lacks reliability because the movement range is suitable.
The assessment lacks validity because repeated scores are similar.
The procedure may be reliable and valid in design, but poor recording reduces accuracy.
feedback: Reliability, validity and accuracy are distinct. Consistency and appropriate content do not compensate for inaccurate measurement or recording.

q: What is the main purpose of a personalised physical activity plan?
options: To match physical activity and sedentary-behaviour strategies to an individual's needs and circumstances
To prescribe the same weekly exercise routine for every participant
To focus only on improving sporting performance
To replace physical activity guidelines with personal preferences
feedback: A personalised plan should be tailored to the individual and promote appropriate physical activity while reducing sedentary behaviour.

q: Which information should be considered when designing a personalised physical activity plan?
options: Only the participant's age and the activities most commonly completed by people in the same age group
Current activity, sedentary behaviour and relevant physiological, psychological and sociocultural information
Only the participant's preferred sport
Only the result of one fitness test
feedback: A strong plan draws on multiple sources of information so that it is safe, appropriate and sustainable.

q: Which action best demonstrates self-management within a physical activity plan?
options: Waiting for someone else to organise every session
Ignoring missed sessions
Recording activity and reflecting on barriers and progress
Changing goals every day without reviewing data
feedback: Self-management involves taking responsibility for behaviours such as planning, monitoring, recording and adjusting activity.

q: Which feature is most important for making a personalised physical activity plan sustainable?
options: Including only high-intensity exercise
Changing activities every session regardless of the participant's preferences, goals, access to facilities or weekly routine
Using the most expensive equipment available
Matching activities to the person's needs, preferences, resources and routine
feedback: Plans are more sustainable when they fit the participant's circumstances, preferences and available resources.

q: Why are clear and measurable goals useful in a personalised physical activity plan?
options: They provide a target that can be monitored and evaluated over time
They guarantee that all barriers will disappear
They remove the need to review the plan
They ensure every participant uses the same activities
feedback: Clear and measurable goals support self-monitoring and make it easier to judge progress and modify the plan.

q: A personalised plan should be designed to promote adherence to which recommendations?
options: Only sport-training recommendations designed for athletes preparing to improve competitive performance over a specific season
Relevant physical activity and sedentary behaviour guidelines
Only muscular-strength recommendations
Only the participant's current routine
feedback: The Study Design requires personalised plans to promote adherence to relevant physical activity and sedentary behaviour guidelines.

q: Which is an example of primary data collected during implementation of a personalised plan?
options: A national report summarising Australian activity trends
A textbook definition of sedentary behaviour
The participant's activity diary and weekly reflections
A government website summarising population trends
feedback: Primary data are collected directly from the participant during the plan, such as activity records and reflections.

q: What is the best basis for evaluating whether a personalised plan has been effective?
