options: Whether the participant enjoyed the first session and felt comfortable
Whether the plan looks detailed
Whether the participant bought new equipment
Comparison of pre- and post-plan data together with participant reflections
feedback: Evaluation should compare baseline and post-implementation data and consider reflections about strengths, limitations and barriers.

q: A participant has a previous knee injury and low current fitness. How should this information influence the plan?
options: Select suitable activities and progression that account for the participant's physical condition
Ignore the injury if the participant is motivated and ask them to complete the original activities without modification
Use only vigorous exercise to improve fitness quickly
Remove all physical activity from the plan
feedback: Physiological information should guide safe and appropriate activity selection, progression and modification.

q: A participant has low confidence about exercising in public. Which strategy best responds to this psychological consideration?
options: Require group exercise immediately
Begin with preferred activities in a comfortable setting and build confidence gradually
Remove all goals from the plan
Increase session difficulty to test commitment
feedback: A plan should respond to psychological factors such as confidence, motivation and self-efficacy.

q: A participant enjoys being active with family but has limited money for organised sport. Which plan feature best addresses these sociocultural factors?
options: A costly gym membership that requires regular travel, specialised equipment and ongoing fees throughout the plan
Solo training at a distant facility
Free or low-cost activities that can be completed with family
Daily sessions requiring specialist equipment
feedback: Social support and financial circumstances are sociocultural considerations that should shape the plan.

q: Which strategy best increases physical activity while also reducing sedentary behaviour?
options: Adding weekend sport while leaving long periods of uninterrupted weekday sitting completely unchanged overall
Completing one long exercise session each month
Replacing all light activity with sitting breaks
Walking during part of the commute instead of remaining seated for the entire trip
feedback: Replacing some seated time with active transport can simultaneously increase physical activity and reduce sedentary behaviour.

q: A participant regularly forgets planned activity sessions. Which self-management strategy is most appropriate?
options: Schedule sessions in a calendar and use reminders
Rely only on memory and decide whether to exercise at the end of each day without using a schedule
Remove all planned activity
Wait until motivation improves before planning
feedback: Planning and scheduling are practical self-management strategies that can support adherence.

q: Why is recording physical activity throughout a personalised plan useful?
options: It guarantees the participant meets every guideline because a written record automatically changes physical activity behaviour
It allows progress, adherence and barriers to be reviewed using evidence
It prevents any future injury
It removes the need for participant reflection
feedback: Records provide primary data that can be used to monitor behaviour and evaluate strengths and limitations.

q: Which goal is most useful for monitoring progress?
options: Be more active sometime
Exercise whenever possible
Complete three planned 30-minute walks this week and record each session
Become much fitter soon
feedback: A specific, measurable and time-framed goal makes progress easier to monitor and evaluate.

q: A participant repeatedly misses evening sessions because of family responsibilities. What is the best modification?
options: Keep the same evening schedule and assume adherence will improve once the participant becomes more motivated
Add more evening sessions
Remove all weekly goals
Move activity to realistic times or use shorter sessions that fit the participant's routine
feedback: A sustainable plan should be adjusted to genuine barriers so that participation is realistic over time.

q: A participant meets their planned exercise target but spends long uninterrupted periods sitting each day. What should the plan do next?
options: Add strategies to break up and reduce sedentary time as well as maintaining physical activity
Ignore sitting because planned exercise automatically cancels the health effects of long daily sedentary periods
Reduce all physical activity
Replace active sessions with more sitting-based hobbies
feedback: Physical activity and sedentary behaviour are separate considerations, so a plan should address both.

q: Which plan is most likely to be sustainable for a busy participant with limited equipment?
options: Daily long sessions that require specialised equipment, fixed travel times and access to facilities that are not always available
Short, flexible activities using accessible locations and minimal equipment
A plan based only on unfamiliar competitive sport
A fixed routine that cannot be changed
feedback: Flexibility, accessibility and fit with the participant's routine support long-term adherence.

q: Which combination would provide the strongest primary data for evaluating a personalised plan?
options: A newspaper article describing exercise benefits together with national statistics about physical activity participation across Australia
A textbook chapter and a government report
Activity records plus the participant's reflections on motivation, barriers and enjoyment
A friend's opinion and a social media post
feedback: Direct activity records and participant reflections provide quantitative and qualitative primary data about implementation.

q: Why should post-plan activity levels preferably be measured using the same method used at baseline?
options: To make the plan longer and ensure the participant completes the same number of activities before and after implementation
To guarantee a positive result
To remove all participant bias
To make pre- and post-plan results more comparable
feedback: Using the same method improves comparability when judging changes from baseline.

q: A participant's activity increases, but they report that the plan is too expensive to continue. What is the best evaluation?
options: The plan shows a benefit but has a sustainability limitation that should be addressed
The plan is fully successful because activity increased
The cost issue should be ignored because it is not physiological
The plan must be stopped permanently
feedback: Evaluation should recognise both positive outcomes and limitations that may affect long-term adherence.

q: A participant enjoys cycling, has access to a bicycle and wants to be more active. Which design choice best supports adherence?
options: Choose activities the participant dislikes but other people commonly enjoy
Include cycling as one appropriate activity within the personalised plan
Require only gym-based exercise
Avoid using existing resources
feedback: Using enjoyable and accessible activities can improve motivation and sustainability.

q: A participant reviews their activity diary each Sunday and adjusts the following week's schedule after identifying barriers. What skill is being demonstrated?
options: Passive participation in which another person reviews the diary, changes the schedule and makes all decisions for the participant
Medical diagnosis
Self-management through monitoring and adjustment
Population-level evaluation
feedback: Reviewing records and modifying behaviour in response to barriers are strong examples of self-management.

q: A participant loses motivation because the plan feels repetitive. Which modification is most appropriate?
options: Increase sedentary time
Make every activity compulsory and keep the same routine even when the participant reports boredom and declining motivation
Remove all monitoring
Introduce suitable variety while retaining activities that support the participant's goals
feedback: Variety can support motivation while the plan remains aligned with the participant's goals and needs.

q: A participant is more active when a friend joins them. How could the plan use this information?
options: Schedule some activities with supportive peers to strengthen adherence
Remove all social activity and require the participant to complete every planned session independently without encouragement from others
Use only solitary exercise
Ignore the influence because it is not physiological
feedback: Peer support is a sociocultural influence that can act as an enabler of physical activity.

q: Which sequence best represents evidence-based personalised planning?
options: Review baseline needs, choose activities, implement them, then evaluate without first setting clear goals
Review baseline needs and barriers, set suitable goals, implement strategies, record data and evaluate
Copy another person's plan without changes
Evaluate before collecting any data
feedback: Personalised planning should use baseline evidence, suitable goals and strategies, implementation data and evaluation.

q: A participant completes most planned sessions but reports increased knee discomfort. What should happen next?
options: Continue unchanged because high adherence is more important than discomfort and the original schedule should always be completed
Increase the activity intensity
Review the plan and modify activities in response to the physiological issue
Ignore the discomfort unless a session is missed
feedback: Evaluation should consider physiological feedback as well as adherence and modify the plan when required.

q: Which finding is best described as a limitation of a personalised plan?
options: The participant enjoys the activities, finds them convenient and reports that they would be willing to continue the plan
The plan uses accessible local facilities
Activity records show improved consistency
The participant cannot sustain the schedule because it conflicts with work commitments
feedback: A schedule that conflicts with ongoing responsibilities reduces sustainability and is a clear limitation.

q: A participant records 90 minutes of planned activity in week 1, 130 minutes in week 2 and 160 minutes in week 3. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The participant's recorded physical activity increased across the three weeks
The participant definitely met every relevant physical activity and sedentary behaviour guideline throughout each of the three weeks
Sedentary behaviour must have decreased
The plan had no limitations
feedback: The data directly support an increase in recorded activity. They do not by themselves prove guideline adherence or reduced sedentary behaviour.

q: A participant completes all weekend sessions but repeatedly misses weekday sessions because of a long commute. Which modification is most appropriate?
options: Increase weekday session duration
Use active transport or shorter sessions that can fit around commuting demands
Remove weekend activity
Add more sessions at times already being missed
feedback: The modification directly addresses the identified time and transport barrier while supporting physical activity.

q: A participant's post-plan step data improve, but their reflections show they disliked the activities and would not continue them. What does this show?
options: The plan has no strengths because the participant disliked it
The plan failed to collect primary data
The plan improved one outcome but has a sustainability limitation
The plan automatically meets all guidelines
feedback: Evaluation can show both a measurable improvement and a limitation affecting long-term adherence.

q: Baseline records show high sitting time during study. The plan adds a short walk after each study block and the participant records fewer prolonged sitting periods. What is the strongest conclusion?
options: The plan only targeted aerobic power and did not attempt to change any aspect of the participant's sedentary behaviour
The participant's sociocultural barriers increased
No evaluation is possible without a fitness test
The strategy appears to have reduced sedentary behaviour during study
feedback: The pre- and post-plan records directly support a reduction in prolonged sedentary behaviour in that context.

q: A participant records each session, rates motivation from 1 to 5 and notes barriers encountered. Why is this useful?
options: It provides primary data about behaviour and psychological experiences that can inform evaluation
It replaces the need to implement the plan because detailed recording and reflection provide enough information without participation
It guarantees the plan is sustainable
It converts all qualitative information into objective data
feedback: Activity records, ratings and reflections provide primary data about what occurred and why adherence may have changed.

q: A participant's goal is to become more active, but the plan contains no scheduled activities, monitoring or review process. What is the main weakness?
options: The participant has too much social support from family and friends, which makes independent self-management impossible to develop
The plan lacks practical self-management structures to turn the goal into action
The plan uses too much primary data
The goal is automatically unrealistic
feedback: Goals need practical strategies such as scheduling, monitoring and review to support implementation.

q: A student has low motivation, enjoys walking with friends and has limited money. Which plan is best justified?
options: A premium gym program completed alone
A demanding solo running plan with no flexibility
Regular free walks with friends, scheduled at realistic times and recorded for review
A plan based on expensive equipment to increase commitment
feedback: This plan addresses motivation, social support, cost, scheduling and self-monitoring in a way that is likely to be sustainable.

q: After four weeks, a participant is more active but still sits for long uninterrupted periods and reports that two planned sessions clash with work. What is the best next step?
options: Keep the plan unchanged because increased activity outweighs sedentary time and scheduling problems
Remove all physical activity
Judge the plan completely ineffective
Retain successful activities, add sedentary-break strategies and reschedule sessions that conflict with work
feedback: Effective evaluation uses both strengths and limitations to guide specific modifications.

q: Which evidence provides the strongest basis for judging the effectiveness of a personalised plan?
options: Comparable pre- and post-plan activity data together with participant reflections about adherence and barriers
The number of pages in the plan and the amount of detail used to describe each scheduled activity
The participant's favourite activity before the plan
A general population statistic collected elsewhere
feedback: Comparable pre/post data plus participant reflections provide direct evidence about outcomes and implementation.

q: A participant's FMA shows no major movement concerns, but they have low self-efficacy and little free time. Which plan design is most appropriate?
options: Use only difficult unfamiliar activities
Begin with achievable preferred activities in short scheduled sessions and monitor progress
Ignore time availability because it is not physiological and require the participant to fit the original schedule around existing commitments
Require long daily sessions to build confidence quickly
feedback: The plan should account for psychological and practical barriers while using achievable, monitorable strategies.

q: A participant reports that exercising with a sibling increased enjoyment and helped them complete more sessions. How should this be interpreted?
options: As evidence that physiological fitness directly caused improved adherence
As proof the plan had no limitations
As primary data showing a sociocultural enabler supported participation
As secondary data about population trends
feedback: The participant's reflection is primary data, and sibling support is a sociocultural enabler.

q: A plan increases physical activity for two weeks, but participation falls when the participant returns to their usual work schedule. Which conclusion is best?
options: The plan is fully sustainable because it worked briefly
The plan should be judged only on the first two weeks
The participant's work schedule is irrelevant
The plan had short-term effectiveness but needs modification to improve long-term sustainability
feedback: A strong evaluation distinguishes short-term success from long-term sustainability and uses barriers to guide future modification.

q: Which statement best describes geographic location as an interpersonal issue in physical activity and sport?
options: It refers only to an individual's motivation to participate.
It describes how where a person lives can influence the opportunities, services and support available to them.
It refers only to climate and weather conditions.
It describes differences in physical ability between participants.
feedback: Geographic location is an interpersonal issue because where people live can shape access to facilities, coaching, transport, competition and other opportunities.

q: Which factor is generally more available in higher-population urban areas?
options: Guaranteed low-cost access to every activity regardless of membership fees, bookings, transport or opening times
Unlimited access to specialist coaches
Equal participation opportunities for all residents
A wider range of sport facilities and competitions
feedback: Urban areas often support more facilities, clubs and competitions because of larger populations, although cost, demand and accessibility can still create barriers.

q: Which statement is most accurate about physical activity opportunities in rural communities?
options: Rural communities can offer strong local connections and natural activity opportunities, but may have fewer specialist services.
Rural communities always have fewer opportunities than urban communities.
Rural communities are unaffected by transport barriers.
Rural communities provide the same sporting options in every location.
feedback: Rural communities may have fewer specialist facilities, coaches or competitions, but can also provide strong community connections and access to natural environments.

q: Why can long travel distances reduce participation in sport?
options: They always reduce an athlete's motivation.
They prevent athletes using online coaching, local clubs or community training options regularly.
They can increase time and transport costs and make regular attendance more difficult.
They automatically make training unsafe.
feedback: Long travel distances can add time, fuel and accommodation costs and compete with school, work or family commitments, reducing regular attendance.

q: Which example best shows terrain acting as an enabler of physical activity?
options: A lack of public transport to a sports centre
High competition fees at a local club
A coastal community providing easy access to surfing
A shortage of qualified coaches
feedback: Terrain can enable particular activities when the local environment provides suitable features, such as coastlines for surfing or trails for mountain biking.

q: Which strategy most directly addresses limited daylight as a barrier to physical activity?
options: Installing suitable lighting on paths and sporting areas
Reducing the number of community facilities so existing venues can be used more efficiently
Restricting outdoor activity to weekends
Increasing competition fees to fund clubs
feedback: Lighting can extend safe opportunities to be active when daylight is limited, especially after school or work.

q: How can socioeconomic circumstances interact with geographic location to affect sport participation?
options: Household income completely determines whether rural or urban communities can provide sporting facilities and coaching
Low income prevents all participation in informal activity.
Geographic distance removes the need for equipment costs.
Travel and accommodation costs can make distant sporting opportunities less affordable.
feedback: When opportunities are far away, travel, fuel and accommodation costs can compound existing financial barriers.

q: Which statement best distinguishes access from inclusion?
options: Access concerns reaching facilities and competitions, while inclusion concerns only whether transport services operate at convenient times for participants.
Access concerns having an opportunity to participate, while inclusion concerns whether people feel welcomed and supported within that opportunity.
Access concerns performance outcomes, while inclusion concerns travel distance only.
Access concerns motivation, while inclusion concerns physical fitness.
feedback: Access is about having opportunities available; inclusion is about whether people can participate meaningfully and feel welcomed, supported and accommodated.

q: Mia lives in a regional town and must travel 120 km each way for specialist gymnastics coaching. She begins missing sessions because of fuel costs and school commitments. Which consequence is most likely?
options: Her geographic location may reduce training frequency and limit skill development.
Her location will improve performance because long travel always develops resilience.
Her location affects inclusion only and cannot affect performance.
Her missed sessions prove she lacks motivation.
feedback: Long travel distances can reduce regular access to coaching. Fewer guided sessions may limit feedback, practice and skill development.

q: A regional athlete has reliable internet but lives three hours from specialist coaching. Which strategy would most directly improve access to regular feedback?
options: Travelling to more distant competitions more often to increase exposure to higher-level opponents and venues
Reducing the number of training sessions
Online coaching using video calls and recorded footage
Waiting until the athlete can relocate
feedback: Online coaching can reduce travel demands and provide more frequent access to specialist feedback when digital connectivity is reliable.

q: Which is the most important limitation of online coaching as a strategy for remote athletes?
options: It guarantees lower performance.
It prevents athletes from receiving any technical feedback.
It can only be used by professional athletes.
It depends on reliable internet, suitable devices and may not replace all practical facilities or face-to-face support.
feedback: Online coaching can improve access but relies on digital infrastructure and cannot replace every practical session, facility or hands-on support need.

q: A regional training hub provides specialist coaching, strength and conditioning support and sports science services closer to athletes' homes. What is the most likely benefit?
options: It removes every financial barrier faced by regional athletes.
It reduces travel demands and may increase regular access to high-quality support.
It guarantees selection into elite teams.
It makes metropolitan facilities unnecessary for every sport.
feedback: Regional hubs can bring specialist services closer to athletes, reducing travel time and improving regular access, but they do not remove every barrier.

q: Why can regional development pathways support performance?
options: They ensure every regional athlete is selected for an elite pathway regardless of performance, readiness, competition results or available places.
They replace the need for local clubs and schools.
They allow athletes to access coaching and competition closer to home before higher-level opportunities require greater travel.
They remove differences in previous sporting experience.
feedback: Regional pathways can provide more regular development opportunities closer to home, supporting skill development and progression.

q: A sporting organisation identifies talented athletes only at metropolitan competitions. What is the main equity concern?
options: Regional athletes with less access to travel and competition may be overlooked despite having potential.
Metropolitan athletes will always have poorer coaching.
Talent identification should never use competition performance because geographic location is the only fair basis for selecting developing athletes.
Regional athletes should automatically be selected.
feedback: If selection occurs only at metropolitan events, athletes facing geographic barriers may have fewer opportunities to be seen.

q: A talented rural athlete qualifies for a state competition but cannot afford travel and accommodation. Which strategy most directly addresses this barrier?
options: More frequent metropolitan competitions requiring additional travel, accommodation, entry fees and time away from home
A higher annual membership fee
Reducing the athlete's training load
A travel scholarship or subsidy
feedback: Travel assistance or scholarships directly reduce the financial cost of accessing distant training or competition opportunities.

q: A small town has unused school courts after hours and no public indoor facility. Which strategy best uses local resources to improve access?
options: Closing the courts to reduce maintenance costs
A partnership allowing community use of the school courts outside school hours
Requiring residents to travel to a larger town
Building a new indoor facility immediately before consulting residents about preferred activities, access needs, schedules, costs or existing resources
feedback: Partnerships between schools, councils and clubs can expand access by sharing existing facilities.

q: Why is community consultation important when planning physical activity opportunities in rural or remote areas?
options: It helps ensure programs reflect local interests, cultural needs and practical barriers.
It guarantees that every resident will participate.
It removes the need for ongoing funding.
It ensures programs reflect local interests, cultural needs and practical barriers consistently.
feedback: Consultation helps planners identify what activities, schedules, facilities and supports are relevant to the local community.

q: Bushfire smoke causes poor air quality across a regional area for several days. Which response best supports continued safe participation?
options: Continue scheduled outdoor sessions while monitoring conditions and change plans only if required.
Cancel all physical activity for the rest of the season.
Use current air-quality information and safely move, modify or postpone sessions when required.
Move every activity indoors regardless of indoor air quality.
feedback: Flexible planning based on current air-quality information can reduce health risk while maintaining opportunities where safe alternatives are available.

q: A community with no natural snow wants to offer snow-sport training. Which option best demonstrates how built environments can modify a geographic barrier?
options: Requiring participants to travel interstate every week even when cost, time and transport reduce regular attendance
Developing an artificial training facility that provides a suitable practice environment
Reducing access to other community sports
Removing all equipment requirements
feedback: Built or artificial facilities can provide alternatives where local terrain or climate does not naturally support an activity.

q: A remote community reports that the only funded sport does not reflect local interests. Participation remains low. Which strategy is most appropriate?
options: Increase advertising for the existing sport without consultation and assume greater promotion will overcome all local participation barriers
Make participation compulsory for young people.
Assume low participation reflects poor motivation.
Co-design a broader program with community members to identify activities they value.
feedback: Community consultation and co-design can improve relevance, inclusion and participation by ensuring activities reflect local interests and needs.

q: A new sports centre is built close to a regional community, but it has high fees and no accessible change rooms. Which conclusion is best?
options: All access and inclusion barriers have been removed.
Only performance can now be affected.
Geographic access has improved, but affordability and inclusion barriers may still limit participation.
Participation must increase because distance is no longer a barrier.
feedback: Being physically close to a facility improves geographic access, but cost and accessibility can still limit meaningful participation.

q: A regional athlete loses two hours of recovery time after every training session because of travel. How could this affect performance?
options: Reduced recovery may contribute to fatigue and lower training quality.
Travel automatically improves aerobic fitness.
Recovery time does not influence performance.
Long travel affects participation but never performance because athletes can always recover fully while travelling home
feedback: Travel demands can reduce available recovery time, potentially increasing fatigue and affecting training quality and performance.

q: Which scenario best demonstrates that urban location does not automatically guarantee access?
options: A rural resident uses local trails for recreation.
A city resident lives near several facilities, but fees are unaffordable and sessions are fully booked.
A coastal resident surfs at a nearby beach.
A regional athlete receives travel support but still has limited access to suitable facilities, qualified coaching and regular competition opportunities.
feedback: Urban areas may have more facilities, but cost, demand, transport schedules and accessibility can still restrict access.

q: Which example is most likely to be an enabler provided by the characteristics of some rural environments?
options: Guaranteed specialist medical services
More professional competitions within walking distance together with frequent public transport and several specialist training centres
Greater public transport frequency
Ready access to natural trails, open spaces or waterways for recreation
feedback: Some rural environments provide natural settings that support activities such as walking, cycling, hiking or water-based recreation.

q: A state sporting body has funds to support regional participation. Which allocation strategy is most ethical?
options: Direct all funding to the largest centre because it has the most participants.
Give equal funding to every community regardless of circumstances.
Use transparent criteria considering need, distance, existing access, community priorities and likely impact.
Fund only athletes already performing at elite level.
feedback: Transparent, needs-based allocation is more likely to improve equitable access than treating communities with different barriers identically.

q: Which action is most clearly a local-level response to geographic barriers?
options: A national sporting body funds a country-wide talent pathway that provides regional coaching, travel assistance and competition opportunities across several states.
A local council upgrades community courts and consults residents about access and scheduling.
An international federation changes global competition rules.
A federal agency develops a national sport policy.
feedback: Local councils and community organisations act at the local level by planning facilities and programs for specific communities.

q: Why might a strategy that works in one country need modification before being used elsewhere?
options: Geographic barriers are identical in every country because distance, climate, infrastructure and community priorities affect all populations in the same way.
International strategies cannot use technology.
Participation is determined only by national income.
Climate, infrastructure, population patterns and community priorities can differ between locations.
feedback: Global strategies need adaptation because geographic, cultural, infrastructural and economic conditions differ between places.

q: Historically, why have metropolitan areas often had greater access to sport and recreation infrastructure?
options: Higher population density has often attracted more facilities, services and funding.
Rural communities have never valued sport and therefore governments have historically avoided investing in facilities outside metropolitan areas.
Regional athletes have always preferred informal activity.
Governments have prohibited facilities outside cities.
feedback: Larger metropolitan populations have often supported greater investment in facilities and services, contributing to historical access differences.

q: A survey finds that 72% of urban adolescents can reach organised sport within 20 minutes, compared with 38% of adolescents in remote communities. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Remote adolescents are less motivated to participate.
Urban adolescents have no barriers to sport participation.
Travel and service availability may create greater access barriers for remote adolescents.
Geographic location alone determines participation because travel time controls access for adolescents.
feedback: The data suggest a difference in geographic access, but they do not prove differences in motivation or show that geography is the only influence.

q: A regional program provides one visiting specialist coach each school term. Attendance rises initially but falls between visits. Which improvement is most likely to make the program more sustainable?
options: Train local coaches and provide ongoing remote support between specialist visits.
Increase the distance athletes must travel.
Replace all local coaches with visiting staff.
Limit the program to athletes who can already afford private coaching and regular travel to metropolitan training centres between visits.
feedback: Building local coaching capacity and providing ongoing support can maintain opportunities between specialist visits.

q: A 16-year-old regional cyclist travels 2.5 hours to a training centre twice a week. After a timetable change, public transport no longer arrives before training starts. Which link best explains the likely impact?
options: Reduced transport access will automatically improve independent training.
The timetable change affects inclusion but cannot affect participation.
Performance will improve because the athlete has more free time.
Reduced transport access may lower attendance, reducing guided training and potentially limiting performance development.
feedback: Transport is part of geographic access. If attendance falls, the athlete may receive less coaching, practice and feedback, which can affect performance.

q: Two remote athletes are offered online coaching. Athlete A has reliable high-speed internet; Athlete B has frequent connection failures and limited data. What does this comparison demonstrate?
options: Online coaching removes geographic barriers equally when identical digital support is offered to athletes.
Digital infrastructure can determine whether technology acts as an enabler or remains a barrier.
Internet access affects motivation but not access.
Both athletes will receive identical coaching experiences.
feedback: Technology can reduce distance barriers only when participants have reliable and affordable digital access.

q: A council survey shows that local teenagers want evening basketball, but the only court has no lighting and buses stop at 6 pm. Which response best addresses the evidence?
options: Build a daytime walking trail without consulting teenagers, even though their stated preference is evening basketball at the existing court.
Increase basketball fees to reduce demand.
Improve court lighting and review transport or scheduling options with the community.
Assume teenagers are not interested in being active.
feedback: The survey identifies specific environmental and transport barriers. A targeted response should address those barriers directly.

q: A region historically had no specialist training centre. A hub opened five years ago and participation has increased, but some communities still travel more than two hours to reach it. Which future strategy is most justified?
options: Evaluate who is still underserved and consider outreach, transport support or additional regional services.
Close the hub because it has not removed every barrier.
Assume the increase in participation means no further action is needed, even when distant communities still face substantial travel barriers.
Require distant athletes to relocate.
feedback: Evaluation should identify who continues to face barriers and guide further targeted strategies rather than assuming one facility solves all access problems.

q: A talented netballer in a rural area can attend specialist coaching only once a month because the nearest program is 180 km away. Which explanation best links geographic location to performance?
options: Distance proves the athlete is less motivated than metropolitan players.
Distance reduces regular access to specialist feedback, which may limit skill development and performance improvement.
Distance affects only social inclusion and cannot influence training.
Monthly coaching guarantees equal development because motivated athletes can successfully reproduce all specialist feedback independently.
feedback: A strong explanation links the geographic barrier to reduced access, then to fewer training and feedback opportunities, and finally to a performance consequence.

q: A remote community has low participation and limited transport. Which proposed strategy is most appropriate?
options: Copy a metropolitan program without modification, deliver it on the same timetable, use the same activities and ignore transport, cultural and facility differences.
Build an expensive facility before identifying community needs.
Focus only on elite talent identification.
Co-design local activities with the community, use existing facilities where possible and provide transport support for opportunities that must occur elsewhere.
feedback: An ethical strategy should respond to identified local barriers and priorities, involve the community and consider sustainable access.

q: A sporting organisation introduces travel grants for regional athletes. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: The grants remove every geographic barrier because reducing travel costs gives regional athletes equal access to facilities, coaching, competition and technology.
The grants can improve performance only, not access.
The grants may improve access by reducing travel costs, but they may not solve limited local facilities, coaching or competition opportunities.
The grants are ineffective unless every athlete receives the same amount.
feedback: Travel grants address affordability and distance-related costs, but geographic disadvantage can involve several interacting barriers.

q: Which statement best compares local and national responses to geographic barriers?
options: Local responses can target specific community facilities and schedules, while national responses can support broader funding, pathways and programs across regions.
Local responses affect participation only, while national responses affect performance only, so the two levels should operate separately rather than coordinate support.
National responses must be identical in every community.
Local responses cannot involve government.
feedback: Local responses can be highly tailored, while national bodies can provide wider funding, policy, pathways and programs. Effective approaches may combine both.

q: Which statement best analyses change over time in geographic access to sport?
options: Geographic barriers disappeared once online coaching became available.
Historical funding patterns have no effect on current opportunities.
Future participation will depend only on athlete motivation.

Historically, many specialist services were concentrated in cities; current regional investment and digital coaching can improve access, but future strategies still need to address unequal infrastructure and connectivity.
feedback: A strong historical-current-future analysis recognises improvement over time while identifying ongoing and emerging barriers.

q: A remote athlete is highly motivated but has unreliable internet, limited local coaching and must travel four hours for competition. Which conclusion best demonstrates an integrated understanding of contemporary issues?
options: Motivation removes the effects of geographic location.
Strong motivation may support persistence, but interpersonal geographic barriers can still restrict access, participation and performance.
Geographic barriers affect access only and cannot influence performance.
The athlete should be excluded from higher-level pathways until local services improve.
feedback: Intrapersonal strengths such as motivation can interact with interpersonal barriers. Motivation alone cannot remove limited services, travel demands or unreliable digital access.

q: Which statement best describes the role of an effective coach?
options: An effective coach focuses only on winning competition results.
An effective coach plans activities, teaches skills, provides feedback and supports athlete wellbeing.
An effective coach avoids changing activities once a session begins.
An effective coach leaves all safety decisions to athletes.
feedback: Effective coaching involves planning, teaching, feedback, inclusion, safety and athlete wellbeing, not performance outcomes alone.

q: Which statement best describes directive coaching?
options: The coach provides clear instructions and demonstrations and makes most immediate decisions.
The athletes independently design the session without coach input.
The coach avoids correcting unsafe technique.
The athletes determine all safety procedures.
feedback: Directive coaching is coach-led and can be useful when clear instruction, demonstrations or immediate safety guidance are required.

q: Which feature is most characteristic of collaborative coaching?
options: The coach makes every decision without explanation.
The coach invites athletes to contribute to goals, feedback and activity choices.
The coach avoids responsibility for safety.
The coach uses the same approach for every athlete.
feedback: Collaborative coaching involves athletes in appropriate decisions, which can support autonomy, motivation and responsibility.

q: Which factor should a coach consider when deciding how much direction or athlete input to use?
options: The athlete's experience, confidence and the complexity or risk of the task
The coach's preference only
The colour of the team's uniform
Whether the session is indoors or outdoors only
feedback: Coaching style should be adapted to the athlete and situation, including experience, confidence, task complexity and safety.

q: What is a key purpose of session planning?
options: To remove the need for feedback during practice
To ensure every athlete completes identical activities
To give activities a clear purpose and organise suitable practice, equipment and supervision
To prevent a coach from adapting activities
feedback: Session planning helps organise purposeful, safe and appropriately challenging activities while allowing opportunities for practice, feedback and adaptation.

q: Which principle is most appropriate when designing a longer-term training program?
options: Keep training difficulty unchanged regardless of progress.
Increase workload whenever an athlete reports fatigue.
Ignore school, work and other commitments.
Increase challenge as athletes become ready while balancing training demands with recovery.
feedback: Program design should use appropriate progression, consider athlete needs and sporting demands, and balance training with recovery and other commitments.

q: Which behaviour best reflects ethical coaching?
options: Using humiliation to increase toughness
Showing favouritism to high-performing athletes
Treating athletes fairly and respectfully while placing wellbeing alongside performance
Encouraging athletes to hide concerns from others
feedback: Ethical coaching involves fair and responsible decisions, respect, dignity, honesty and concern for athlete wellbeing.

q: What does safeguarding athletes primarily involve?
options: Protecting coaches from all criticism
Keeping athlete concerns within the coaching group
Allowing coaches to set their own private communication rules
Protecting athletes from harm, including abuse, bullying and harassment
feedback: Safeguarding focuses on protecting athletes from harm and requires clear boundaries, reporting pathways and responsible organisational practices.

q: A beginner is learning a potentially dangerous gymnastics skill for the first time. Which coaching approach is most appropriate initially?
options: Clear direct instructions and demonstrations with close attention to safety
Allow the athlete to design the skill progression independently
Ask the athlete to choose any technique they prefer
Avoid correcting technique until the athlete becomes experienced
feedback: Beginners learning unfamiliar or risky skills may benefit from directive coaching because clear instructions and demonstrations can support learning and safety.

q: An experienced athlete understands the basic skill and is working on tactical decision-making. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use only repeated commands and remove athlete input throughout every training session.
Invite the athlete to discuss options, set goals and reflect on decisions.
Stop the athlete asking questions during practice.
Choose every goal without explaining the reason.
feedback: Experienced athletes may benefit from collaborative coaching that supports autonomy, reflection and problem-solving.

q: A coach begins a session with direct safety instructions, then later asks experienced athletes to help choose practice activities. Why is this appropriate?
options: It removes the coach's responsibility for safety.
It guarantees every athlete will perform at the same level after every coaching session.
It adapts coaching style to suit different stages of the session and athlete needs.
It proves directive coaching is always superior.
feedback: Effective coaches can change approaches within a session, using direct instruction when safety or clarity is needed and collaboration when athlete input is appropriate.

q: A new participant is unsure what equipment is needed and worries that an activity will be too difficult. Which coaching response best supports access and inclusion?
options: Tell the participant to watch until they can complete the full activity.
Use the same task without modification because fairness requires identical treatment for participants throughout training.
Ask another participant to make all decisions for them.
Explain what to expect, identify available equipment and adapt the activity to the participant's needs.
feedback: Clear information and appropriate adaptations can help beginners access sessions and participate meaningfully.

q: A coach consistently gives the most skilled athletes more practice time and ignores beginners. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Beginners may feel less valued and become less likely to continue participating.
Beginners will automatically become more motivated.
Performance opportunities will become more equitable for beginners and experienced athletes alike.
The coaching environment will become more inclusive.
feedback: Favouritism can weaken inclusion, confidence and continued participation, particularly for less experienced athletes.

q: A training session has long queues and athletes spend most of the time waiting for one piece of equipment. Which change would best improve the session?
options: Add more explanation without changing the activity structure, equipment setup or waiting times significantly.
Reduce waiting time by reorganising space, equipment or activity stations to increase practice opportunities.
Extend the session so athletes can wait longer.
Remove feedback to save time.
feedback: Good session planning should maximise meaningful practice opportunities and organise equipment and space efficiently.

q: An athlete reports persistent fatigue and declining enjoyment during a demanding training block. Which response best reflects appropriate program design?
options: Increase training volume to improve resilience.
Ignore the fatigue because the program was planned in advance for everyone.
Monitor the athlete's response and adjust training demands or recovery where needed.
Remove all future competition goals.
feedback: Program design should respond to athlete feedback, fatigue and recovery rather than rigidly applying the same training load.

q: A coach increases task difficulty only after athletes demonstrate readiness. What principle does this best demonstrate?
options: Favouritism
Safeguarding reporting
Overtraining
Appropriate progression
feedback: Appropriate progression means increasing challenge as athletes become ready, rather than advancing too quickly or keeping tasks unchanged.

q: Which feedback is most likely to support skill development?
options: "Your balance improved; now follow through towards the target."
"That was terrible. Try harder."
You always make the same mistake, so stop now.
"Just copy the best athlete."
feedback: Effective feedback is specific, constructive and gives the athlete a clear next step that can be applied in practice.

q: A coach humiliates an athlete after every mistake. Which outcome is most likely?
options: The athlete will automatically become more independent and perform consistently under pressure in competition.
The athlete may fear making mistakes, lose confidence and become less willing to participate.
The athlete will necessarily improve faster.
The coaching relationship will become more inclusive.
feedback: Humiliation can create fear, reduce confidence and discourage athletes from asking questions, seeking help or continuing participation.

q: Which coaching practice is most likely to support continued participation?
options: Using excessive pressure and public criticism to ensure athletes understand that competition results come first.
Removing athlete feedback from session planning
Recognising effort and improvement while providing achievable and varied activities
Criticising mistakes publicly
feedback: Enjoyment, achievable challenge, supportive relationships and recognition of progress can encourage athletes to remain involved.

q: A coach pressures athletes to use a banned substance because it may improve results. Which principle is being violated?
options: Collaborative decision-making and athlete autonomy during training program design and goal setting
Session organisation
Skill progression
Ethical coaching and fair play
feedback: Ethical coaching requires honesty, fair play and athlete wellbeing. Winning does not justify harmful or dishonest practices.

q: A junior coach sends private late-night messages to one athlete and asks that the messages remain secret. What is the most appropriate response?
options: Follow the organisation's safeguarding and reporting procedures and use transparent communication channels.
Ignore the behaviour if the messages mention sport.
Ask the athlete to keep monitoring the coach.
Keep the concern within the coaching team until clear proof of physical harm has been collected.
feedback: Secret or inappropriate private communication is a safeguarding concern and should be taken seriously and reported through appropriate channels.

q: Which communication practice best supports professional boundaries with junior athletes?
options: Using private disappearing messages
Using approved club channels at appropriate times with relevant adults able to view communication
Contacting athletes through personal social media accounts late at night, provided the messages only discuss training and competition.
Asking athletes not to share messages
feedback: Transparent, sport-related communication through approved channels helps protect athletes and coaches.

q: A coach wants to transport a junior athlete alone to an event. Which practice is most appropriate?
options: Keep the arrangement informal because it is sport-related.
Ask the athlete not to mention the arrangement.
Use appropriate approval procedures and obtain required parent or carer consent before transport arrangements.
Transport the athlete without informing anyone if the journey is short and the coach considers the arrangement convenient and safe.
feedback: Professional boundaries require appropriate approval and consent for transport arrangements involving junior athletes.

q: An athlete reports feeling uncomfortable about a coach's behaviour but has no proof of harm. What should a club official do first?
options: Dismiss the concern until evidence is provided.
Tell the athlete to confront the coach alone.
Promise that the concern will remain completely secret so the athlete feels comfortable continuing to talk.
Take the concern seriously, listen calmly and follow appropriate reporting procedures.
feedback: Safeguarding concerns should be taken seriously even without proof, with appropriate support and reporting procedures followed.

q: Which action best demonstrates a sporting club taking responsibility for safe coaching?
options: Providing codes of conduct, coach education, supervision and clear reporting pathways
Assuming a screening check guarantees safe behaviour and therefore removing the need for supervision, training or reporting procedures
Leaving each coach to create their own safeguarding rules
Responding only after serious harm occurs
feedback: Safe coaching environments require organisational systems such as recruitment checks, education, supervision, codes of conduct and accessible reporting.

q: Why is a Working with Children Check not sufficient by itself to ensure athlete safety?
options: It applies only to elite sport.
Screening does not replace ongoing supervision, training, safe practices and reporting systems.
It guarantees that no safeguarding concerns can arise once a coach has passed the screening process.
It removes the need for codes of conduct.
feedback: Screening is one safeguard, but organisations still need supervision, education, professional boundaries and effective complaint and reporting processes.

q: Which is the best example of a national-level coaching response?
options: A local club adopts a safeguarding policy and requires every coach to follow its communication, supervision and reporting procedures.
A parent gives feedback after a game.
A national sporting organisation develops coach education and safeguarding guidance for clubs across the country.
One athlete changes their personal goal.
feedback: National sporting organisations can set expectations, education and safeguarding guidance that support more consistent coaching standards across regions.

q: Which statement best describes a historical change in coaching practice?
options: Coaching has always used the same athlete-centred approach.
Safeguarding concerns exist only in modern sport.
Safeguarding concerns exist only in modern sport because historical athletes were more resilient, accepted strict coaching methods and did not experience the same risks from power imbalances.
Harsh, win-at-all-costs methods were more likely to be accepted in some sporting environments, while current practice places greater emphasis on athlete wellbeing and safeguarding.
feedback: The lesson contrasts historical acceptance of harsh methods with current athlete-centred approaches that place greater emphasis on wellbeing, boundaries and safeguarding.

q: A beginner group is learning a new contact skill. The coach first demonstrates the skill and gives clear safety instructions. Later, once athletes are competent, the coach asks them to suggest tactical variations. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The coach is appropriately adapting between directive and collaborative coaching as athlete needs change.
The coach should have used collaboration only from the beginning because athlete choice is always safer than direct instruction when learning contact skills.
The coach has removed responsibility for athlete safety.
The coach is using inconsistent methods that cannot support learning.
feedback: The scenario shows coaching style being adapted to suit safety, skill level and athlete readiness.

q: A coach records athlete fatigue, enjoyment and progress each week. When fatigue rises and performance falls, the coach reduces training load and increases recovery. What does this best demonstrate?
options: Using the same program regardless of feedback because consistency is more important than individual athlete responses.
Monitoring athlete responses and making individual program adjustments
Replacing coaching judgement with athlete preference
Reducing standards whenever training becomes difficult
feedback: Good program design includes monitoring athlete responses and adapting training and recovery when needed.

q: A club requires all junior-team communication to occur through an approved group platform visible to parents and relevant officials. What is the main safeguarding benefit?
options: It prevents athletes from ever speaking directly with coaches.
It guarantees that no safeguarding issue can occur as long as parents can view every message exchanged on the platform.
It creates transparent professional communication and reduces opportunities for secret one-to-one contact.
It removes the need for reporting procedures.
feedback: Transparent communication channels support professional boundaries, although they do not replace broader safeguarding systems.

q: Two athletes attend the same session. One requires modified equipment to participate meaningfully, while the other does not. Which coaching response best supports inclusion?
options: Require identical equipment and task conditions because fairness means every participant should complete precisely the same activity without individual adjustments.
Exclude the athlete needing modification from the activity.
Reduce both athletes to the easiest version of the task.
Provide suitable modifications based on individual needs rather than requiring identical conditions for everyone.
feedback: Inclusive coaching may require different supports so participants can take part meaningfully and fairly.

q: After a month, athletes report that they enjoy training less because the coach criticises mistakes publicly and gives little positive feedback. Attendance begins to fall. Which relationship is best supported?
options: Harmful communication may reduce enjoyment and confidence, which can lower continued participation.
Public criticism always improves motivation.
Attendance changes cannot be influenced by coaching behaviour.
Positive feedback affects performance only and cannot influence confidence, enjoyment, trust or whether athletes continue attending sessions.
feedback: Coaching behaviour can influence enjoyment, confidence, trust and the likelihood that athletes continue attending.

q: A sporting organisation replaces a traditional win-at-all-costs coaching program with athlete-centred education, safeguarding training and regular athlete feedback. Which interpretation is strongest?
options: The organisation has removed the need for performance goals.
The organisation reflects a shift from historically accepted harsh practices towards current approaches emphasising wellbeing, inclusion and accountability.
The change proves historical coaching was always unsafe.
The organisation can now stop reviewing coaching practices because athlete-centred education and safeguarding training permanently remove the possibility of harmful coaching behaviour.
feedback: The change reflects the broader move towards athlete-centred coaching, safeguarding and ongoing review while still allowing performance goals.

q: An experienced netballer helps set training goals and suggests practice activities while the coach retains responsibility for safety. Which explanation best links this approach to participation?
options: The athlete now controls all safety decisions.
Collaborative coaching guarantees improved performance.
Collaborative coaching can increase autonomy and ownership, which may strengthen motivation and encourage more consistent participation.
The coach should avoid athlete input because experienced athletes need more direct instruction and fewer opportunities to make decisions about their own training.
feedback: A strong explanation links collaborative coaching to autonomy and ownership, then to motivation, enjoyment and continued participation.

q: A junior athlete tells a club official that a coach has been sending private late-night messages and asking the athlete not to tell anyone. Which response is most appropriate?
options: Keep the messages confidential unless physical harm is proven.
Keep the messages confidential unless physical harm is proven because reporting unverified concerns could unfairly damage the coach's reputation.
Ignore the messages if they relate to performance.
Take the concern seriously, support the athlete and follow safeguarding and reporting procedures.
feedback: Safeguarding concerns should be taken seriously, athletes should be supported, and appropriate reporting processes should be followed.

q: A coach increases training volume every week despite several athletes reporting fatigue, reduced enjoyment and declining performance. Which evaluation is most accurate?
options: The program lacks appropriate monitoring and recovery adjustment, which may undermine participation, wellbeing and performance.
The program is effective because training workload should continue increasing whenever athletes become tired, even if enjoyment and performance are declining.
The athletes should ignore fatigue because progression must be identical.
The issue relates only to motivation, not program design.
feedback: Effective program design should use monitoring and recovery to guide progression rather than increasing demands regardless of athlete responses.

q: Which statement best compares local and national responsibilities for safe coaching?
options: National bodies manage every local coaching interaction directly.
National bodies can provide broad education and safeguarding expectations, while local clubs must apply them through everyday coaching, supervision and reporting processes.

Local clubs do not need their own safeguarding processes if a national organisation has published guidance, because national standards automatically control everyday coach behaviour in every training environment.
Safeguarding is only a national responsibility.
feedback: National organisations can provide consistent guidance, but local clubs must implement safe practices in daily coaching environments.

q: Which statement best analyses future implications for coaching?
options: Technology will eventually remove the need for coach judgement, athlete feedback and privacy safeguards because objective performance data will provide all information required to design safe and inclusive training programs.
Future coaching will focus only on performance data.
Coaching is likely to become more individualised, with greater use of athlete feedback and technology, while coaches still need to protect privacy, wellbeing and inclusion.
Safeguarding will become less important as technology improves.
feedback: The lesson identifies more individualised coaching, increased use of feedback and technology, continued education and ongoing responsibility for privacy, inclusion and wellbeing.

q: A highly motivated athlete trains under a coach who uses humiliation, excessive control and public criticism. Which conclusion best demonstrates an integrated understanding of contemporary issues?
options: Motivation prevents coaching behaviour from affecting the athlete because highly motivated performers can maintain confidence, enjoyment and participation regardless of humiliation, control or public criticism.
Coaching affects performance only and cannot influence participation.
Harmful coaching is acceptable if competition results improve.
Strong motivation may support persistence, but harmful interpersonal coaching can still reduce confidence, enjoyment, inclusion and continued participation.
feedback: Intrapersonal strengths such as motivation can interact with interpersonal coaching influences. Harmful coaching may still affect confidence, wellbeing, inclusion and participation.

q: Which statement best describes sports technology?
options: It refers only to equipment used by elite athletes.
It applies innovations such as equipment, digital tools and monitoring devices to physical activity and sport.
It describes media coverage of sporting events.
It refers only to online exercise programs.
feedback: Sports technology includes equipment, digital tools, monitoring devices and other innovations used to support physical activity, participation and performance.

q: How can online exercise programs improve access to physical activity?
options: They can reduce travel barriers by allowing people to participate at suitable times and locations.
They guarantee that every participant has reliable internet access.
They remove all costs associated with physical activity.
They make face-to-face activities unnecessary.
feedback: Online programs can reduce transport and scheduling barriers, but access still depends on suitable devices, internet and other individual circumstances.

q: Which information can a wearable device commonly collect during physical activity?
options: Only an athlete's motivation
Only competition results
Heart rate, distance and speed
Only coach observations
feedback: Wearable devices can collect data such as heart rate, distance and speed, which may help monitor effort and progress.

q: What is a key benefit of video analysis in sport?
options: It guarantees that an athlete will improve performance.
It replaces the need for coaching judgement.
It removes the need for repeated practice.
It can reveal movement details and support specific feedback on technique.
feedback: Video analysis can help athletes and coaches review movement and provide more specific feedback, but it still requires interpretation and practice.

q: How can sports media influence behaviour?
options: By shaping what people see, value and consider possible, which may affect sporting choices
By guaranteeing participation in every sport shown
By removing financial barriers to physical activity
By determining sporting ability
feedback: Media can influence behaviour by shaping beliefs, awareness and perceptions about sport, which may encourage or discourage participation.

q: What does representation in sports media refer to?
options: How often athletes train
Who is shown in media and how they are portrayed
How much equipment costs
How coaches design training programs
feedback: Representation concerns who is visible in sports media and how athletes or groups are portrayed.

q: Which practice best supports ethical collection of athlete data?
options: Collecting information without explaining its purpose
Sharing all data with sponsors automatically
Obtaining informed consent and explaining what is collected, why it is collected and who can access it
Keeping data indefinitely regardless of need
feedback: Ethical data collection requires informed consent, transparency about purpose and access, and appropriate privacy protections.

q: Why should performance data be interpreted in context?
options: Because technology data are always inaccurate
Because athlete feedback should replace all data
Because coaches should avoid using numerical information
Because a single score may be influenced by training demands, athlete condition or measurement error
feedback: A single score does not explain the whole performance. Training conditions, athlete feedback and measurement limitations should also be considered.

q: A participant lives far from a gym but has reliable internet and a suitable device. Which strategy would most directly reduce the access barrier?
options: An online exercise program that can be completed at home
Travelling further to attend a more expensive facility each week
Waiting until a local gym is built
Reducing physical activity opportunities
feedback: Online exercise can reduce travel demands and allow participation at home when suitable devices and internet are available.

q: A participant cannot use standard equipment because of a physical disability. Which response best supports inclusion?
options: Require the participant to use the standard equipment
Consult the participant and provide suitable adapted equipment
Remove the participant from the activity
Provide an easier activity without consultation
feedback: Inclusive technology should respond to individual needs and be developed with participant input so meaningful participation is possible.

q: A fitness app awards points for completing activity goals. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Gamification guarantees long-term participation because points and rewards motivate all participants in every situation.
Points remove all access barriers.
Gamification may increase engagement for some participants, but it will not motivate everyone equally.
Competition always improves confidence.
feedback: Gamification can support motivation and engagement, but individual responses vary and some people may find comparisons discouraging.

q: A club moves all registrations online. Which action would best support equitable access?
options: Require every participant to register digitally because online systems are equally accessible to all members
Increase registration fees to fund the website
Limit registrations to existing members
Offer assistance and an offline registration option for people who cannot use the digital system
feedback: Digital systems can improve convenience, but offering assistance and offline alternatives helps people who face digital access barriers.

q: A coach uses GPS data to adjust an athlete's training load. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use the GPS data together with athlete feedback and coach observation.
Use GPS data as the only source for every training decision.
Ignore unusual readings if the athlete reports fatigue.
Assume all devices are perfectly accurate.
feedback: Wearable data should be interpreted alongside athlete feedback and professional judgement because devices and individual responses can vary.

q: A smartwatch records a slower running speed than usual during a session with different drills, and the athlete reports feeling tired. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: The athlete's performance has definitely declined.
The result should be interpreted alongside the session demands and athlete feedback.
The smartwatch must be inaccurate.
The athlete should immediately stop training until the device records their speed.
feedback: The result needs context. Different drills and fatigue may explain the change, so the technology should not be interpreted in isolation.

q: A coach shows an athlete slow-motion footage of their technique and identifies one specific change to practise. Why is this likely to be useful?
options: It guarantees immediate performance improvement.
It removes the need for coach-athlete discussion because footage provides certainty.
It provides focused feedback the athlete can apply during repeated practice.
It makes physical practice unnecessary.
feedback: Video can make technical details easier to see and support specific, manageable feedback that can then be practised.

q: Why can device placement affect the usefulness of sports technology data?
options: It changes an athlete's motivation automatically.
It determines whether the athlete is included in a team.
It removes the need for calibration.
It can alter the accuracy or consistency of recorded measurements.
feedback: Poor placement or signal quality can affect readings, so coaches should consider measurement reliability when interpreting data.

q: How can improved equipment design influence performance?
options: It may improve fit, control or movement efficiency, although performance still depends on skill and preparation.
It guarantees success for anyone who uses the equipment because technological improvements determine performance in competition.
It removes the need for training.
It affects access but never performance.
feedback: Equipment can support performance through improved fit, control or efficiency, but it does not determine success by itself.

q: A club introduces expensive tracking devices that require annual subscriptions. What is the main equity concern?
options: Every participant will benefit equally because devices provide identical opportunities regardless of income or access.
Some participants may be unable to afford the technology and therefore miss similar feedback opportunities.
Technology costs affect performance only.
Subscriptions automatically improve inclusion.
feedback: Cost can create unequal access to technology and the development opportunities it may provide.

q: A wearable records an athlete's location, sleep and training load. Which organisational practice is most appropriate?
options: Share the information with all coaches, administrators and sponsors so anyone involved in the program can use it when needed.
Collect the data without telling the athlete.
Explain what data are collected, obtain consent, restrict access and store the information securely.
Keep all data permanently even when no longer needed.
feedback: Sensitive athlete data should be collected transparently, with informed consent, limited access and secure storage.

q: Why might a governing body regulate the use of sports technology in competition?
options: To prevent any future technological development
To guarantee equal funding for every athlete
To require every competitor to use the newest approved equipment so performance differences between athletes are eliminated
To balance innovation with fairness and the requirements of the sport
feedback: Equipment rules can help maintain fair competition while still allowing appropriate innovation.

q: A teenager sees repeated media stories suggesting that a particular sport is only for one type of person. What is a possible effect?
options: The teenager may believe they do not belong in the sport and become less likely to participate.
The teenager will definitely join the sport because repeated media exposure always changes beliefs and overcomes every other participation barrier.
The coverage will remove access barriers.
The media message cannot influence behaviour.
feedback: Media messages can shape beliefs about who belongs in sport, which may encourage or discourage participation.

q: How can diverse athlete representation support inclusion?
options: It guarantees equal funding for every sport because broader representation automatically produces identical sponsorship and media investment across all competitions.
It can help viewers see people like themselves participating and strengthen a sense of belonging.
It removes transport barriers.
It ensures every viewer becomes physically active.
feedback: Seeing diverse athletes represented respectfully can challenge stereotypes and help more people feel that participation is possible and welcoming.

q: How can increased media coverage indirectly support athlete performance?
options: It guarantees better performance because athletes who receive more media coverage always train more effectively and recover more successfully.
It removes the need for recovery.
It may attract sponsorship that funds coaching, equipment or other development resources.
It prevents public pressure.
feedback: Media exposure can attract funding and sponsorship, which may improve access to resources that support athlete development and performance.

q: An athlete receives repeated online abuse after a competition. What is a possible consequence?
options: The athlete will automatically become more confident because public criticism always increases resilience and improves motivation to remain involved in sport.
The abuse improves inclusion.
Online comments cannot affect participation.
The athlete may feel unsafe or unwelcome and withdraw from public or sporting involvement.
feedback: Online abuse can affect confidence, wellbeing, inclusion and continued participation.

q: A club post promotes beginner sessions and clearly lists costs, times and available support. How can this influence access?
options: It can help potential participants understand how and when to join.
It guarantees that everyone can afford the program once clear information about fees, schedules and support is posted online.
It removes the need for facilities.
It affects performance only.
feedback: Clear participation information can reduce uncertainty and help people identify suitable opportunities.

q: Why can increased quality coverage of female athletes influence beliefs about sport?
options: It guarantees equal pay immediately because positive media coverage automatically forces sporting organisations to distribute all resources equally between athletes.
It can challenge gender stereotypes by focusing on sporting skill and achievement.
It removes every structural barrier.
It ensures all sports receive identical funding.
feedback: Respectful, skill-focused coverage can challenge stereotypes and broaden beliefs about who belongs in sport.

q: Media coverage and junior registrations for a sport both increase over the same period. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
options: Media coverage definitely caused every new registration because no other factor can influence whether young people become aware of, access or join a sport.
Registrations cannot be influenced by media.
The increases are associated, but the information alone does not prove that media coverage caused the rise in registrations.
All access barriers must have been removed.
feedback: An association between media coverage and registrations does not prove causation. Other factors such as fees, facilities or new programs may also contribute.

q: Which media practice is most ethical when sharing an athlete's personal story?
options: Share private information if it may attract more views.
Use an athlete's image without permission if the post promotes sport.
Ignore online abuse unless sponsorship is affected.
Obtain consent, respect privacy and present the athlete fairly.
feedback: Ethical sports media should respect consent, privacy and fair representation, and organisations should respond to harmful online behaviour.

q: A club's wearable data show that an athlete's weekly running distance fell by 15%. The athlete was completing rehabilitation sessions instead of normal training. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The lower distance should be interpreted in the context of the changed training program.
The athlete has definitely become less fit because any reduction in weekly running distance proves a decline in physical capacity.
The wearable has failed.
The athlete should return immediately to full training.
feedback: Changes in training context can explain changes in recorded data, so the result should not be interpreted in isolation.

q: A community club introduces GPS watches. Athletes gain useful training feedback, but each member must pay an additional annual fee and several families cannot afford it. Which evaluation is strongest?
options: The watches should be compulsory because data are useful.
