The watches may support training, but the cost barrier can reduce equitable access to the benefit.
The cost is irrelevant because useful performance technology benefits all athletes equally once a club decides the information is valuable.
The club should stop using all technology.
feedback: A strong evaluation recognises both the performance benefit and the access limitation created by cost.

q: A women's competition receives more media coverage over three years. During the same period, spectator awareness and junior registrations also rise. What is the best interpretation?
options: Media coverage is proven to be the only cause of increased registrations because awareness and participation rose during the same period.
Junior registrations must have increased because sponsorship increased.
The variables increased together, but the information does not prove that media coverage caused every change.
The data prove that all gender-equity barriers were removed.
feedback: The data show an association, not proof of causation. Other changes may also have influenced awareness and registrations.

q: An athlete receives extensive media attention before a major event. Sponsorship increases, but the athlete reports disrupted concentration and reduced recovery time because of interviews. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: Media attention affects sponsorship only and cannot influence concentration, recovery, confidence or other aspects of athlete performance.
Public attention always improves concentration.
The athlete should avoid all media permanently.
Media exposure can create both performance benefits and performance pressures.
feedback: Media exposure may bring resources and recognition while also increasing scrutiny, pressure and demands on training or recovery.

q: An online fitness platform adds captions, clear demonstrations and seated exercise options. Which outcome is most likely?
options: The changes may improve inclusion by making activities usable for a wider range of participants.
The changes guarantee that all participants will join because captions and seated options remove every remaining access and inclusion barrier.
The platform no longer needs internet access.
The changes affect performance only.
feedback: Accessible instructions and adapted activity options can help more people participate meaningfully.

q: Sports monitoring once relied heavily on stopwatches and written records, while current athletes can use wearable devices and automated analysis. Which future issue is most important to consider as technology develops further?
options: Whether athletes should stop using human judgement entirely once automated systems can process larger amounts of performance data.
Privacy, fairness, access and the accuracy or bias of automated feedback
Whether all technology should be banned from sport
Whether digital tools can replace physical training
feedback: Future sports technology may expand opportunities, but ethical safeguards must develop alongside innovation, particularly around privacy, fairness, access and automated decision-making.

q: A professional club uses GPS technology to monitor workload. The system provides detailed feedback but is expensive and stores personal location and health data. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The technology benefits every athlete equally because objective data automatically remove differences in affordability, digital access and individual interpretation.
The technology should replace coach observation.
The technology may support individualised training, but cost, privacy, accessibility and data interpretation must be considered.
The technology affects performance but cannot affect access or inclusion.
feedback: A strong evaluation weighs the performance benefit against concerns about affordability, privacy, accessibility and interpretation.

q: A women's sporting competition receives increased media coverage, more people become aware of the competition and junior registrations rise. Which explanation is strongest?
options: Media coverage alone caused every new registration.
Participation rose because media coverage removes cost, transport and facility barriers and therefore guarantees that every interested viewer can access the sport.
Coverage can influence performance but not participation.
Greater visibility may influence beliefs and awareness and contribute to participation, but other access factors may also affect registrations.
feedback: Media can influence beliefs, awareness and behaviour, but participation also depends on factors such as cost, transport, facilities and available programs.

q: A new piece of equipment improves performance but is available only to well-funded teams. Which response best addresses the issue?
options: Governing bodies should consider whether the technology creates an unfair advantage and whether rules are needed to protect competition equity.
All teams should be required to buy the technology immediately because equal rules are achieved whenever every competitor is expected to purchase the same equipment regardless of cost.
Technology should never be used in sport.
Performance improvements always justify unequal access.
feedback: Ethical evaluation should consider who benefits, who misses out and whether regulation is needed to balance innovation with fairness.

q: Which statement best compares local and global influences of sports technology and media?
options: Local technology affects access only, while global technology affects performance only, because the scale at which technology is used completely determines which sporting outcome it can influence.
Local clubs may use affordable tools to improve access and communication, while global sport may face wider issues involving international exposure, funding differences and equipment regulation.
Global media reaches everyone equally.
Local clubs cannot use digital technology.
feedback: Local and global contexts can use similar technologies differently, and the scale of access, funding, exposure and regulation varies.

q: Which statement best analyses change over time in sports media?
options: Sports media has always operated in the same way.

Digital media has removed all inequalities in sports coverage because every athlete, competition and audience now has equal access to online platforms, sponsorship, reliable internet, respectful representation and the same opportunity to create and distribute content.

Traditional media once gave audiences fewer choices and broadcasters greater control, while digital platforms now allow wider participation in content creation but also create new issues such as online abuse and privacy.
Future media will no longer influence beliefs or behaviour.
feedback: A strong historical-current-future analysis recognises both expanded access and new ethical challenges created by digital media.

q: A young athlete follows a popular online training account, buys an expensive wearable and copies a demanding program without professional advice. Which conclusion best demonstrates an integrated understanding?
options: Popular online advice is reliable whenever many people follow it because large audiences prove the program is safe, suitable for individual needs and supported by accurate evidence.
Technology guarantees that the copied program is appropriate.
Media and technology cannot interact to influence participation or performance.
Media may influence behaviour, while technology can provide useful feedback, but cost, suitability, interpretation and the reliability of online advice still matter.
feedback: Media can shape behaviour and technology can support monitoring, but benefits depend on trustworthy advice, appropriate interpretation, individual needs and equitable access.

q: Which statement best describes institutional and structural inclusion in sport?
options: It means every participant must receive exactly the same support.
Sporting organisations use rules, leadership and resources in ways that help different people access, belong, participate and progress.
It refers only to the design of sporting equipment.
It applies only to elite sporting organisations.
feedback: Institutions and structures include organisations, rules, leadership and resource allocation. Their decisions can create or remove barriers to sporting involvement.

q: What is the main difference between equality and equity in sport?
options: Equality provides the same support, whereas equity responds to different needs and barriers.
Equality changes support for each participant, whereas equity treats everyone identically.
Equality relates only to performance, whereas equity relates only to access.
Equality and equity mean exactly the same thing.
feedback: Equality means providing the same opportunity or resource. Equity recognises that different barriers may require different support to create fair opportunities.

q: Why is community consultation important when designing inclusive sporting programs?
options: It guarantees that every participant will agree with the final program.
It removes the need for organisational responsibility.
It helps organisations identify actual needs and barriers before making decisions.
It allows leaders to avoid reviewing the program later.
feedback: Consultation helps organisations understand the needs, priorities and barriers experienced by participants and communities.

q: Which feature best reflects a culturally safe sporting environment?
options: Every cultural group is expected to follow identical practices without discussion.
Only elite athletes are asked about cultural needs.
Concerns are ignored unless participation numbers fall.
Participants' identities are respected and there are clear processes for responding to racism or discrimination.
feedback: Cultural safety involves respect for identity, freedom from racism or humiliation, meaningful consultation and clear responses to concerns.

q: Which statement best reflects an inclusive approach to physical diversity?
options: Assume that a physical disability determines the participant's sporting ability.
Ask the participant about their goals and useful adjustments, then adapt support where needed.
Remove challenging activities from anyone who uses adapted equipment.
Use identical equipment for every participant regardless of need.
feedback: Inclusive practice starts with the participant's strengths, goals and preferences rather than assumptions about ability.

q: Which strategy can support a participant who needs extra processing time?
options: Use short instructions, demonstrations, processing time and repeated practice.
Give several new instructions at once to increase independence.
Reduce all activities to the easiest possible level.
Avoid giving feedback so the participant is not confused.
feedback: Clear language, step-by-step demonstrations, processing time and repeated practice can support understanding while maintaining appropriate challenge.

q: How can discriminatory language affect gender and sexually diverse participants in sport?
options: It has no effect if the participant remains registered.
It improves motivation by making sport more competitive.
It can weaken safety and belonging and may reduce participation or performance.
It affects spectators but not athletes.
feedback: Discriminatory language and harassment can reduce belonging, discourage attendance and create distraction that affects performance.

q: Why are registration numbers alone insufficient to judge whether a sporting environment is inclusive?
options: They cannot provide any information about participation.
They measure performance instead of participation.
They are useful only for national organisations.
They show who joins but not necessarily whether participants feel respected, heard or meaningfully involved.
feedback: Participation data are useful, but participant experiences are also needed to judge safety, belonging and meaningful inclusion.

q: A club's registration information is available only in complex English, and several families cannot understand how to enrol. Which strategy most directly addresses the barrier?
options: Keep the existing information and ask children to translate it.
Provide plain-language and translated information with registration assistance.
Increase the registration fee to fund more training sessions.
Limit enrolment to families already familiar with the club.
feedback: Accessible and translated information can reduce a communication barrier and improve access to the registration process.

q: Several participants regularly miss training because sessions clash with important cultural or religious commitments. What is the most inclusive response?
options: Consult participants and consider flexible scheduling where practical.
Keep the schedule unchanged because equality requires identical treatment.
Remove participants who cannot attend every session.
Assume the participants are not committed to the sport.
feedback: Consultation and flexible scheduling can address a structural barrier without making assumptions about commitment.

q: A player reports repeated racial abuse at training. Which organisational response is most appropriate?
options: Ignore the report unless several other players complain.
Ask the player to solve the issue privately with the person involved.
Use clear reporting procedures, respond consistently and support the affected participant.
Wait to see whether the player stops attending.
feedback: Organisations should respond to racism through clear procedures, consistent action and support. Ignoring reports can undermine trust and safety.

q: A regional organisation wants to develop a new sport program with a local Aboriginal community. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use a successful program from another community without changes.
Complete the program first and request feedback after launch.
Use cultural symbols in promotion without seeking permission.
Co-design the program with local community leaders and organisations so local priorities shape planning and delivery.
feedback: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities are diverse. Meaningful inclusion requires local voice, partnership and co-design rather than assumptions or one-size-fits-all programs.

q: A club publishes an inclusion policy but provides no staff training, funding or reporting process. What is the main limitation?
options: The policy automatically creates an inclusive environment once published.
The policy may have little practical effect because responsibilities and resources have not been established.
The policy should focus only on elite athletes.
Written policies are never useful in sport.
feedback: Inclusive policies need implementation through resources, staff training, clear responsibilities, reporting processes and ongoing review.

q: A club has a small inclusion budget. Participant feedback identifies transport costs as the main reason some members cannot attend training. Which use of the funding is most equitable?
options: Prioritise transport assistance for participants affected by the identified barrier.
Divide the money equally among every registered member regardless of need.
Spend the full budget on promotional posters.
Reserve all funding for the highest-performing team.
feedback: Equitable resource allocation responds to identified barriers. If transport is preventing attendance, targeted assistance can improve participation.

q: A wheelchair user cannot enter a sporting venue because the only entrance has stairs. Which change most directly improves access?
options: Offer encouragement and ask the participant to practise climbing stairs.
Move all activities to a more difficult location.
Provide an accessible entrance and clear pathways through the venue.
Ask another participant to carry the wheelchair.
feedback: Accessible entrances and pathways remove a structural barrier that prevents a participant from entering and using the venue.

q: A participant has difficulty controlling the standard ball used in a skills session. Which response is most inclusive?
options: Remove the participant from skill practice.
Use the ball because equal treatment requires every participant to use identical equipment.
Make every activity easier for the whole group.
Consult the participant and trial suitable equipment adjustments while maintaining an appropriate challenge.
feedback: Adaptations should respond to individual needs while preserving choice, meaningful participation and opportunities to progress.

q: A participant finds multi-step spoken instructions difficult to remember. Which coaching adjustment is most appropriate?
options: Repeat instructions faster and more loudly so the participant receives the same information as everyone else.
Demonstrate one step at a time, allow practice and check understanding before adding the next step.
Exclude the participant from complex skills.
Give the participant an unrelated activity.
feedback: Breaking instructions into manageable steps, demonstrating, allowing practice and checking understanding can support skill learning and performance.

q: A participant can complete most activities independently but sometimes needs assistance. What approach best supports inclusion?
options: Ask what assistance is useful and provide support without taking over tasks the participant can manage.
Provide assistance for every task so the participant never needs to make independent choices during sessions.
Speak only to the participant's support person.
Remove all challenging activities.
feedback: Inclusive support respects participant choice and independence while providing assistance where it is genuinely useful.

q: Why can offering mainstream, adapted and specialist participation options support inclusion?
options: Require every participant with support needs to choose a specialist program because specialists always provide safer participation.
It prevents participants from changing programs over time.
It can provide meaningful choice so participants can select settings that suit their goals and support needs.
It removes the need to consult participants.
feedback: Different participation settings can support different goals and needs. The key is meaningful participant choice rather than automatic placement.

q: A club hears repeated homophobic comments in the change rooms. Which response best supports inclusion?
options: Ignore the comments unless a player leaves the club.
Ask affected players to avoid the change rooms.
Require players to disclose their orientation before support is offered so the club can respond consistently.
Set and enforce clear expectations for respectful behaviour, provide a reporting pathway and address the comments.
feedback: Organisations should address discriminatory language consistently, provide accessible reporting and protect participant privacy.

q: Which action best respects the privacy of a gender-diverse participant?
options: Share the participant's identity with the team so everyone can prepare appropriate support together.
Ask what support is helpful and avoid pressuring the participant to disclose personal information.
Require personal details before allowing participation.
Discuss the participant's identity publicly to promote inclusion.
feedback: Inclusive practice respects privacy, individual choice and the participant's preferences about what information is shared.

q: A participant with disability is welcomed into social sessions but is never considered for advanced coaching despite strong performance. What is the main inclusion issue?
options: Access to development and performance pathways is being restricted by assumptions rather than relevant ability.
The participant already has full inclusion because registration provides equal access to every development opportunity.
Advanced coaching should be limited to participants without disability.
Development pathways are unrelated to inclusion.
feedback: Inclusion extends beyond entry. Fair opportunities to develop, compete, coach, officiate and lead should be based on relevant skills and goals rather than assumptions.

q: How can diverse representation in club leadership improve structural inclusion?
options: It guarantees every leadership decision will satisfy all members because diverse representation removes the need for further consultation.
It removes the need for community consultation.
It can bring a wider range of experiences into decisions about policies, resources and programs.
It affects leadership but cannot influence participation.
feedback: Representation can help decision-making reflect a wider range of experiences, although meaningful inclusion also requires consultation, action and review.

q: Why might a local club partner with community organisations when developing an inclusion program?
options: Partnerships allow the club to avoid direct consultation because community organisations can speak accurately for every participant and family.
Community organisations should make all club decisions.
Partnerships are useful only for one-off events.
Community partners can help identify priorities, build trust and connect the club with interested families.
feedback: Local partnerships can combine knowledge, relationships and resources, especially when maintained through shared planning and ongoing feedback.

q: What is an important role for a national sporting body in promoting inclusion?
options: Design one identical national program for every community because consistent delivery is more important than local consultation or adaptation.
Provide guidance, education and resources that support inclusive practice across state and local organisations.
Focus only on national-team selection.
Leave all inclusion decisions to individual athletes.
feedback: National bodies can support inclusion through policy, education, resources and guidance, but local implementation still needs to respond to participant circumstances.

q: An international competition increases the visibility of athletes with disability. Why does this not prove that local sport is fully inclusive?
options: Elite visibility can challenge assumptions, but local barriers such as cost, facilities and coaching may still restrict participation.
International success automatically removes community barriers because visible elite athletes prove that facilities, coaching, cost and attitudes are equally supportive everywhere.
Local clubs are unaffected by access and inclusion issues.
Visibility matters only to spectators.
feedback: Elite success and visibility can influence beliefs, but accessible community opportunities, resources and support are still necessary for local inclusion.

q: How can historical exclusion continue to influence current participation?
options: Historical exclusion has no current effect once organisations change their written rules because trust is restored immediately by policy reform.
Only current funding levels influence participation.
Past discriminatory practices can affect trust in sporting institutions and willingness to engage with unfamiliar organisations.
Historical issues affect performance but not access.
feedback: Historical exclusion can shape current trust and engagement. Sustained practical change, community voice and accountability are needed to rebuild confidence.

q: A club's registrations rise after an inclusion initiative, but several participants report that they are still excluded from decisions. What is the best interpretation?
options: The initiative is fully successful because registrations increased.
Participant feedback should be ignored because subjective experiences are less important than the number of people who register.
The club should remove the inclusion initiative.
Registrations suggest improved access or participation, but participant feedback shows inclusion still needs attention.
feedback: Multiple forms of evidence are needed. Registrations can show who joins, while participant feedback provides evidence about belonging and meaningful involvement.

q: A club charges every junior the same fee. A review finds that some families cannot afford registration or equipment. Which change best demonstrates equity?
options: Keep the same fee because identical treatment ensures every family receives an equal and therefore fair sporting opportunity.
Offer targeted fee assistance and equipment loans based on identified financial barriers.
Increase all fees so the club can buy more equipment.
Remove families who cannot pay on time.
feedback: Equity responds to different barriers. Targeted financial support can make the sporting opportunity genuinely accessible.

q: A sporting organisation plans a program for several Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities. Leaders propose using exactly the same activities, timetable and promotion in every location. What is the strongest concern?
options: Communities have different priorities and circumstances, so local consultation and co-design are needed.
National organisations should use the same program everywhere because consistency is more important than differences between local communities.
All communities prefer different sports.
Promotion should occur only after the program finishes.
feedback: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities are diverse. Local voices should guide priorities, delivery and review rather than assuming one program suits everyone.

q: A club reports higher attendance among participants with disability after buying adapted equipment. Feedback shows that several participants still cannot access the upstairs meeting room. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: The club is fully inclusive because higher attendance proves that all facility, communication and participation barriers have been removed.
The adapted equipment should be removed.
Participation has improved, but a remaining facility barrier means the club should continue reviewing inclusion.
Facility access does not affect inclusion.
feedback: Improved attendance is positive evidence, but participant experience can reveal remaining barriers that still require action.

q: A basketball player with an intellectual disability performs well in familiar drills but becomes confused when several new instructions are given at once. Which response best supports performance?
options: Lower every drill permanently because participants with intellectual disability should always receive easier activities regardless of skill.
Remove the player from tactical activities.
Give the same rapid instructions more loudly.
Use short step-by-step instructions, demonstrations and repeated practice before combining the movements.
feedback: Breaking a task into clear steps and allowing practice supports understanding and skill execution without unnecessarily reducing challenge.

q: A teenager stops attending training after repeated transphobic comments from teammates. Which outcome is most directly illustrated?
options: The athlete lacks commitment to training because attendance decisions are determined mainly by personal motivation rather than team behaviour.
Discriminatory behaviour has weakened inclusion and contributed to reduced participation.
The comments improved team cohesion.
The issue affects access only.
feedback: Harassment can undermine safety and belonging, causing participants to reduce or stop their involvement.

q: A club consults a culturally diverse community before launching a program, changes session times and communication methods, and then reviews attendance and participant feedback. Why is this approach strong?
options: It combines community voice, practical action and evidence-based review rather than treating consultation as a one-off activity.
It guarantees every participant will remain because consultation and schedule changes automatically remove all other access, inclusion and participation barriers.
It removes the need for future changes.
It focuses only on participation numbers.
feedback: Meaningful consultation should influence decisions and be followed by review using both participation data and participant experiences.

q: A club has an inclusive registration policy but allocates its best facilities, coaches and development funding to the same established group each year. Which evaluation is most appropriate?
options: The club is fully inclusive because open registration means every member has an equal opportunity to access the best facilities, coaches and development resources.
Resource allocation affects performance only and cannot influence inclusion.
The club's formal access may be inclusive, but resource allocation can still create structural inequity in participation and performance opportunities.
Equal registration rules guarantee equitable development pathways.
feedback: Institutional inclusion depends on more than registration. How facilities, coaching and funding are distributed can affect who participates, develops and progresses.

q: Which statement best compares inclusion strategies across local and national sport?
options: Local clubs should follow national programs without adapting them because consistent implementation across all communities is more important than responding to different local barriers and participant needs.
National bodies influence performance but not access or inclusion.
Local organisations cannot contribute to structural change.
Local clubs can adapt directly to participant needs, while national bodies can provide broader policy, education and resources that support consistent inclusive practice.
feedback: Local organisations can respond to specific community needs, while national organisations can influence systems through policy, education, resources and leadership.

q: Which statement best analyses inclusion in sport over time?
options: Historical exclusion becomes irrelevant once a modern inclusion policy is introduced because written rules immediately restore trust, remove structural barriers and guarantee fair participation opportunities.
Historical exclusion can shape current trust, current inclusive practices can reduce barriers, and future progress depends on sustained consultation, resources and accountability.
Current inclusion means future barriers cannot emerge.
Future inclusion depends only on increasing registrations.
feedback: A strong time-based analysis links historical effects, current strategies and the need for sustained future action and review.

q: A sporting organisation wants to improve inclusion for a group that reports high costs, poor access to facilities and little voice in decisions. Which strategy is most comprehensive?
options: Consult the group, target resources at the identified barriers, improve facility access and include members in meaningful decision-making.
Run a promotional campaign without changing resources or facilities.
Provide exactly the same support to every member because equality ensures fairness even when participants report different barriers involving cost, facilities and decision-making.
Wait for participation to increase before making structural changes.
feedback: A strong ethical response addresses the specific barriers identified by participants and combines practical resources with meaningful community voice.

q: A club provides translated registration information, respectful coaching, flexible session times and fair access to advanced coaching. Which sequence best explains the likely outcomes?
options: Translated information improves performance directly, while advanced coaching affects access only, because each strategy influences a single sporting outcome and cannot affect other stages of involvement.
Flexible session times guarantee inclusion regardless of coaching behaviour.
Translated information can improve access, respectful coaching can strengthen inclusion, flexible times can support participation, and advanced coaching can support performance.
All four strategies influence exactly the same sporting outcome.
feedback: Different strategies can affect different stages of sporting involvement, from gaining access through to belonging, regular participation and performance development.

q: After an inclusion program, registrations rise by 20% and retention improves, but participant interviews identify ongoing racism and limited leadership opportunities. Which judgement is strongest?
options: The program is fully successful because registrations increased.
The interviews should be ignored because numerical data are more reliable.
The program has failed completely because any remaining barrier proves that increased registrations and retention have no value and that none of the inclusion strategies worked.
The program has improved some participation outcomes, but inclusion remains incomplete because participant experiences and structural opportunities still show barriers.
feedback: Evaluation should use multiple forms of evidence. Improved registrations and retention show progress, while reported racism and limited leadership opportunities show that further action is needed.

q: Which statement best describes gender equity in sport?
options: Giving every participant exactly the same resources in every situation
Providing fair sporting opportunities and support by addressing barriers linked to gender
Focusing only on equal participation numbers
Providing extra support only to elite athletes
feedback: Gender equity focuses on fairness. It may require different supports where gender-related barriers affect access, inclusion, participation, performance or progression.

q: How can gender stereotypes influence sporting participation?
options: They can shape beliefs about which sports or roles are suitable for particular genders.
They guarantee that athletes choose sports that match their abilities.
They affect leadership but not participation.
They only influence professional sport.
feedback: Gender stereotypes can affect confidence, aspirations, support and perceptions of belonging, which may influence sporting choices and participation.

q: Why can training-time allocation be a gender equity issue?
options: Training times affect only spectators.
All training times provide identical opportunities.
Less suitable training times can make regular attendance and preparation more difficult for some groups.
Training schedules are unrelated to participation.
feedback: The quality and timing of access matter. Repeated allocation of less suitable times can reduce participation, preparation and performance opportunities.

q: What does a gender pay gap in sport refer to?
options: A difference in training volume between teams
A difference in athlete age
A difference in competition rules between sports
A difference in sporting earnings between genders
feedback: A gender pay gap is a difference in earnings between genders. Sporting income may include salaries, prize money and sponsorship.

q: What does representation in coaching refer to?
options: How many athletes attend training
Who holds coaching positions and has opportunities to progress into senior coaching roles
How much media coverage a competition receives
How coaches measure fitness
feedback: Coaching representation concerns who holds coaching roles and who has genuine opportunities to enter and progress through coaching pathways.

q: Why does representation on sporting boards and committees matter?
options: These bodies influence funding, facilities, policies and priorities that shape sporting opportunities.
Board members only organise social events.
Leadership representation affects performance but not access.
Boards do not influence resource allocation.
feedback: Decision-making bodies influence policies, resources, facilities and priorities, so representation can affect whose needs and experiences are considered.

q: How can lower sporting income affect an athlete's performance?
options: It automatically improves motivation.
It guarantees reduced participation.
It may require extra paid work, reducing time for training, sleep or recovery.
It affects income but cannot affect preparation.
feedback: Lower sporting income may create additional work demands, reducing preparation, sleep or recovery and potentially affecting performance.

q: Why are participation numbers alone insufficient to judge gender equity?
options: Participation data cannot show any useful information.
Gender equity only concerns coaching.
Equal participation automatically proves equal opportunity.
Equity also involves resources, pay, treatment, leadership and influence over decisions.
feedback: Higher participation can show progress, but gender equity also requires examining pay, resources, treatment, leadership and decision-making influence.

q: A club gives its men's teams most evening training slots while women's teams usually train very early in the morning. What is the main equity concern?
options: Morning training always improves performance.
The scheduling may make regular attendance and recovery more difficult for the women's teams.
The issue affects media coverage only.
Equal numbers of teams make the schedule equitable even when quality of times differs.
feedback: Less suitable training times can create structural barriers by affecting attendance, sleep, recovery, preparation and continued participation.

q: A women's program receives less access to accredited coaches, medical support and specialist equipment than the men's program. Which outcome is most likely?
options: Reduced access to development resources may limit participation, preparation and performance opportunities.
The programs remain equitable because both groups still compete in organised competition.
Only athlete confidence can be affected.
Resource allocation cannot influence sporting outcomes.
feedback: Unequal access to coaching, medical support and equipment can affect both participation and performance pathways.

q: A female athlete earns less sporting income and takes evening work to meet living costs. She then sleeps less before morning training. Which link is strongest?
options: Paid work automatically improves sporting discipline.
Income affects participation but cannot affect performance because financial circumstances sit outside training and competition.
Lower sporting income can reduce recovery, increasing fatigue and potentially reducing training or competitive performance.
Sleep is unrelated to sporting income.
feedback: Financial circumstances can influence sleep and recovery, which are intrapersonal factors that may affect concentration, coordination and sporting execution.

q: When comparing gender pay in sport, why is it important to identify what type of earnings are being compared?
options: All forms of sporting income are equivalent because they contribute to an athlete's financial support.
Prize money is the only meaningful measure.
Only professional athletes receive sporting income.
Annual salary, pay per match, prize money and sponsorship measure different aspects of sporting income.
feedback: A valid comparison must identify the measure being used because annual earnings, match payments, prize money and sponsorship are not equivalent.

q: A qualified woman is repeatedly overlooked for senior coaching roles while less experienced candidates are appointed through informal networks. Which issue is most evident?
options: The candidate lacks access to participation.
Biased recruitment and limited networks may restrict coaching progression.
The issue is mainly about athlete pay.
Informal recruitment improves equity by identifying strong coaching candidates.
feedback: Informal networks and biased assumptions can create structural barriers to coaching progression even when candidates have relevant skills.

q: Which strategy would best support more women to progress into senior coaching roles?
options: Provide mentoring, practical experience, accessible development opportunities and transparent recruitment.
Appoint one woman because representation alone resolves coaching progression barriers.
Limit coaching courses to current senior coaches.
Use personal networks to fill vacancies.
feedback: Effective pathways combine development, experience, mentoring and transparent recruitment based on relevant coaching skills.

q: A club committee has 12 members but only one woman. Why might this matter for gender equity?
options: One woman guarantees all perspectives are represented because committee membership automatically gives equal influence over decisions fairly.
Committee composition affects only administration.
Limited representation may mean barriers affecting women and girls receive less attention in resource and policy decisions.
Participation levels make leadership representation irrelevant.
feedback: Decision-making bodies influence funding, facilities and policy. Limited representation can mean some experiences and barriers are less visible in those decisions.

q: Which situation best demonstrates meaningful representation rather than token representation?
options: A woman is appointed but excluded from major decisions.
A committee advertises its diversity while women hold positions but remain excluded from funding decisions.
One leadership position is created without any responsibilities.
Women hold leadership roles and have genuine influence over decisions about funding, facilities and policy.
feedback: Representation is meaningful when people have genuine influence over decisions, not simply when they occupy a position.

q: A girl is repeatedly told that her chosen sport is 'for boys'. What is a likely effect?
options: The stereotype strengthens motivation by encouraging athletes to prove others wrong.
The stereotype may reduce belonging, confidence or willingness to continue participating.
The comment affects access to facilities only.
The comment cannot influence sporting behaviour.
feedback: Gender stereotypes can shape confidence, aspirations and belonging, which may influence continued participation.

q: A club wants to increase participation among women and girls. What should it do first?
options: Consult participants about their goals, interests and barriers before designing changes.
Assume all women prefer the same type of program because shared gender always creates identical sporting goals and barriers.
Create only competitive programs.
Copy the men's program without modification.
feedback: Consultation helps organisations understand specific barriers and preferences instead of assuming all women and girls have the same needs.

q: Players report repeated sexist comments from staff. Which organisational response is most appropriate?
options: Ignore the comments unless players leave.
Ask players to tolerate the comments because maintaining staff authority is more important than responding to individual concerns.
Address the behaviour consistently, provide clear reporting pathways and support affected participants.
Focus only on improving facilities.
feedback: Gender equity also depends on respectful environments. Organisations should respond consistently to sexist behaviour and provide clear support and reporting processes.

q: A club builds new change rooms for women but continues to give women's teams the least suitable training times. What is the best evaluation?
options: The club has achieved full gender equity because new facilities automatically resolve scheduling, culture and participation barriers.
Training times cannot influence participation.
Facilities matter but organisational decisions do not.
The new facility may improve access and comfort, but scheduling still creates a participation barrier.
feedback: Infrastructure can remove one barrier, but gender equity also depends on how opportunities such as training times are allocated.

q: Which action is most appropriate for a local club trying to improve gender equity?
options: Wait for a national body to solve local issues because clubs have little influence over everyday sporting opportunities.
Review training times, coaching, facilities and resources with participant input, then monitor whether changes improve involvement.
Focus only on elite athletes.
Measure success using registrations alone.
feedback: Local clubs directly control many everyday opportunities, so they can use participant feedback to improve scheduling, resources, coaching and support.

q: How can a national sporting body support gender equity?
options: Provide sustained funding, leadership pathways, policy direction and monitoring across the sport.
Set national gender-equity goals without providing resources because clear targets alone are enough to change local practice.
Focus only on national-team results.
Leave leadership development entirely to individuals.
feedback: National bodies can influence pathways, resources and expectations across the sporting system through funding, development, policy and accountability.

q: How can global female sporting role models contribute to gender equity?
options: They automatically remove local cost and facility barriers because visible success changes every community sporting environment.
They guarantee equal pay in all sports.
They can broaden aspirations by showing that women can succeed as athletes, coaches and leaders.
They make local programs unnecessary.
feedback: Visible global role models can challenge stereotypes and broaden aspirations, but local opportunities and resources are still required.

q: How can historical restrictions on women's sport influence current opportunities?
options: Historical exclusion has no current effect once participation rises because modern opportunities replace earlier structural patterns.
Only current athlete ability matters.
Past restrictions affect media but not resources.
Established networks, funding patterns and leadership structures may continue to favour men's sport.
feedback: Historical exclusion can shape current structures, networks and investment patterns even after formal restrictions have been removed.

q: A sport has greatly increased the number of women participating, but women remain rare in senior coaching and board roles. What is the best conclusion?
options: Gender equity has been fully achieved because equal athlete participation is the most important indicator of fairness.
Participation has improved, but leadership equity remains incomplete.
Leadership representation is unrelated to gender equity.
More participation automatically produces equal leadership.
feedback: Progress in playing opportunities does not necessarily mean equivalent progress in coaching, leadership, pay or decision-making.

q: A women's team is allocated inconvenient training times and several players miss sessions. One player reports lower confidence before competition. Which relationship is best shown?
options: An interpersonal scheduling issue can influence an intrapersonal factor such as confidence and then affect performance.
Confidence is an interpersonal factor because it is shaped by the behaviour and decisions of sporting organisations.
Training schedules are intrapersonal factors.
Scheduling cannot influence performance.
feedback: Organisational conditions are interpersonal influences that can affect individual confidence, preparation and ultimately performance.

q: A club finds that women's teams receive less access to accredited coaches. Which response is most ethical?
options: Keep the current allocation because it reflects tradition.
Give accredited coaches to the highest-profile men's team because performance potential should always outweigh gender-equity concerns in allocation.
Review coach allocation transparently and ensure access is based on relevant sporting needs rather than gender.
Ask athletes to organise their own coaching.
feedback: An ethical strategy should address the identified inequity through transparent, relevant and fair allocation processes.

q: Why should a sporting organisation review gender-equity initiatives over time?
options: Every gender-equity strategy should remain unchanged once introduced because consistency is more important than participant feedback.
To replace participant feedback with registration numbers.
Because targets guarantee success without monitoring.
To determine whether barriers are actually reducing and whether strategies need adjustment.
feedback: Monitoring helps organisations judge whether actions are working, identify continuing barriers and adjust strategies as circumstances change.

q: A review shows that men's teams receive 70% of prime training slots and most strength-and-conditioning support, while women's teams report lower attendance. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: The women's teams are less committed.
Unequal resource allocation may be contributing to participation differences and should be reviewed.
Prime training times affect performance but not participation.
The allocation is equitable because both groups can train, even if one receives consistently better times and support.
feedback: The resource pattern may be creating structural barriers. A strong conclusion links the allocation to possible effects without assuming a single cause.

q: Two athletes compete at the same level. One receives lower sporting income, works additional evening shifts and reports fatigue at morning training. Which explanation best links the factors?
options: Lower sporting income may increase outside work demands, reducing recovery and potentially affecting training quality and performance.
The athlete's fatigue proves lower motivation.
Pay affects finances but cannot affect sporting outcomes because athletes can separate employment demands from training and recovery.
Working more hours always improves resilience.
feedback: This demonstrates how an interpersonal financial inequity can influence intrapersonal recovery and fatigue, which may then affect sporting performance.

q: A national sport reports that women make up 48% of participants but only 18% of head coaches. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
options: The sport has achieved gender equity because near-equal athlete participation matters more than representation in senior coaching.
Coaching representation cannot affect sporting opportunities.
High athlete participation does not necessarily mean equitable representation in senior coaching pathways.
The figures prove discrimination caused every appointment.
feedback: Participation and coaching representation are different indicators. The data identify an imbalance but do not by themselves prove a single cause.

q: A board increases women's representation from 15% to 45%, but women report that major funding decisions are still made informally by a small existing group. What is the best evaluation?
options: Gender equity is complete because greater numerical representation guarantees equal influence over every major board decision.
Board influence is unrelated to resource allocation.
Informal decision-making always improves fairness.
Numerical representation has improved, but meaningful influence over decisions may still be limited.
feedback: Representation should include genuine influence. Headcounts alone do not show whether decision-making power has changed.

q: A sport that historically restricted women's competition now has strong participation growth, but leadership and pay gaps remain. Which statement best reflects change over time?
options: Historical restrictions are irrelevant because current participation growth proves earlier inequalities no longer affect sporting structures.
Playing opportunities have improved, but historical patterns may still influence current leadership and financial structures.
Current participation proves future equity.
Pay and leadership are unrelated to historical structures.
feedback: Progress can occur in one area while historical structural patterns continue in others, such as leadership, funding or pay.

q: After introducing equitable training schedules and leadership mentoring, a club reports higher retention of women players and more women applying for coaching roles. What is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: The changes are associated with positive participation and pathway outcomes, but ongoing monitoring is still needed.
The strategies caused every improvement because retention and coaching applications increased immediately after the changes were introduced.
The club no longer needs participant feedback.
Retention alone proves equal pay.
feedback: The evidence suggests positive change, but organisations should avoid claiming single-cause certainty and should continue monitoring multiple indicators.

q: A community association gives men's teams preferred court times, greater medical support and more experienced coaches. Several women players reduce their involvement. Which explanation is strongest?
options: The players' reduced involvement proves they lack motivation because structural resources cannot meaningfully influence sporting participation decisions.
Medical support influences performance only.
Structural resource inequities may reduce access to quality preparation, weaken inclusion and contribute to lower participation.
Equal registration rules make the association equitable.
feedback: The scenario shows how institutional decisions about resources can affect several sporting outcomes, including inclusion, participation and performance opportunities.

q: A national organisation wants to increase women and gender-diverse people in coaching and decision-making positions. Which strategy is most comprehensive?
options: Appoint one person without changing existing systems because a visible appointment is sufficient to demonstrate structural reform.
Rely on current leaders' personal networks.
Focus only on athlete participation.
Use transparent recruitment, mentoring and development pathways, set measurable representation goals and review progress regularly.
feedback: Structural change requires transparent recruitment, development opportunities, measurable goals and accountability rather than isolated appointments.

q: Which statement best compares gender-equity action at local, national and global levels?
options: Only global organisations can affect gender equity because local clubs and national bodies lack sufficient authority to change funding, facilities, coaching pathways, leadership opportunities or everyday sporting experiences.
Local clubs can change everyday resource allocation, national bodies can shape pathways and policy, and global organisations can influence standards, advocacy and visibility.
Local clubs influence participation but not resources.
National bodies have no role in leadership pathways.
feedback: Gender equity can be influenced at multiple levels, with different organisations affecting everyday access, system-wide pathways and broader standards or advocacy.

q: Which statement best analyses gender equity in sport across time?
options: Historical exclusion can shape current resources and leadership, while future progress requires sustained investment, representation and accountability.
Past inequalities disappear once participation numbers rise because current involvement completely replaces the effects of historical exclusion today.
Current media visibility guarantees future equity.
Future equity depends only on athlete performance.
feedback: A strong time-based analysis connects historical structures to current inequalities and identifies sustained future strategies rather than assuming progress is automatic.

q: A women's team receives poor training times, leading to missed sessions, reduced confidence and less consistent competition performance. Which explanation best demonstrates the interrelationship?
options: Confidence caused the poor training schedule.
Performance cannot be influenced by attendance because confidence, preparation and skill execution are separate from training opportunities.
An interpersonal scheduling inequity reduces practice opportunities, which can affect intrapersonal confidence and then influence performance.
The scheduling issue is purely intrapersonal.
feedback: The strongest explanation shows the chain from an interpersonal organisational condition to an intrapersonal response and then a sporting outcome.

q: A club reports equal registration numbers for men and women, but women receive less funding, fewer prime training times and hold few leadership roles. What is the strongest judgement?
options: The club has achieved gender equity because registrations are equal.
Funding and leadership are unrelated to gender equity.
Equal participation automatically produces equal performance.
Equal participation numbers do not demonstrate full gender equity because resources, opportunities and decision-making influence remain unequal.
feedback: Gender equity must be judged across multiple dimensions. Equal participation does not compensate for continuing inequities in resources, opportunities or influence.
